title: Hiker's unexplained death exposes deadly alcohol withdrawal risk many don't recognize
summary: Alcohol withdrawal seizures can strike 24 to 48 hours after the last drink, turning wilderness settings into life-threatening traps for heavy drinkers.
story: The actor explained that his wife gave him an ultimatum when it came to his drinking, which got him to stop.

When hiker Joanna Ruth Shields, 37, was found dead near Sykes Hot Springs in California’s Ventana Wilderness, initial speculation pointed to foul play, according to a press release from the Monterey County Sheriff's Office.
However, official coroner's reports revealed her cause of death to be probable alcohol withdrawal seizures brought on by chronic alcohol use disorder.
Friends who were hiking with Shields said she had gone to the river that morning. A short time later, one of them found her unresponsive in the water, according to reports.
IS DRINKING EVERY DAY ALCOHOLISM? EXPERTS EXPLAIN WHERE CULTURE AND ADDICTION COLLIDE

"This is a probable seizure that occurred as a result of chronic alcohol use disorder, but there was nothing that stood out that indicated any type of criminal activity," Andres Rosas, commander and the primary public information officer for the Monterey County Sheriff's Office, told KSBW 8.
Given the results of the investigation and forensic examination, no further investigation is taking place.
The recent death of a Big Sur hiker was ruled a probable case of fatal alcohol withdrawal seizures, exposing a dangerous and often hidden medical crisis. (iStock)
The incident highlights a little-known danger of severe alcohol dependence, as suddenly stopping alcohol can trigger life-threatening neurological events.

Alcohol acts as a depressant on the central nervous system. When someone drinks heavily over a prolonged period, the brain adapts by ramping up chemical signals to keep bodily systems functioning, according to experts.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
When alcohol is abruptly stopped, that blocker on the central nervous system is removed. The brain then enters a state of dangerous overexcitation, leading to severe hyperarousal.
Withdrawal symptoms typically begin within six to 24 hours after the last drink, with the risk of seizures peaking between 24 and 48 hours.
Alcohol withdrawal can quickly progress from tremors, sweating and anxiety to severe seizures and a condition called delirium tremens. (iStock)
In wilderness settings or isolated locations, a sudden seizure can result in immediate loss of consciousness, trauma, respiratory arrest or an inability to seek emergency care, experts note.
Clinical guidelines from the National Institutes of Health categorize alcohol withdrawal by the following key progression stages.
Stage 1 (6 to 12 hours post-drink)

This may include minor withdrawal symptoms, including insomnia, tremors, anxiety, gastrointestinal upset, headache, diaphoresis (excessive sweating), heart palpitations, anorexia, nausea, tachycardia (abnormally fast resting heart rate) and hypertension.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Stage 2 (12 to 24 hours post-drink)
This stage is marked by visual, auditory or tactile hallucinations.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Stage 3 (24 to 72 hours post-drink)

People in this stage may experience sudden loss of consciousness accompanied by severe muscle contractions (seizures). Another potential symptom is delirium tremens, a medical emergency involving extreme agitation, fever, racing heart, hyperthermia and cardiac instability.
Attempting to detox without medical supervision can result in sudden loss of consciousness, trauma and death, experts warn. (iStock)

Health agencies, including the National Institutes of Health, strongly advise that individuals with a history of heavy drinking or prior withdrawal episodes never attempt to detox alone or in remote settings.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Medical detox programs use tailored medication protocols to safely taper brain activity and prevent seizures.

Help is available for people struggling with alcohol use disorder. The Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration National Helpline provides free, confidential treatment referrals 24 hours a day at 1-800-662-4357.

title: Older adults taking 5 or more prescription drugs face higher risk of death, study finds
summary: Each additional prescription medication was linked to a 7% increase in death risk among older adults, raising urgent questions about deprescribing.
story: Older adults who walked at a significantly faster speed than their peers were about half as likely to develop cognitive impairment, according to Dr. Joe Verghese, MD, neurologist at Stony Brook Medicine.

Older adults who take five or more prescription medications face a significantly higher risk of death compared to those taking fewer drugs, according to a study published in the Journal of the American Geriatrics Society.
The research highlights the growing concern over polypharmacy, the medical term for taking five or more daily prescriptions, and its long-term effects on aging populations.
Led by Dr. Alexander Chaitoff of the University of Michigan School of Medicine, researchers analyzed national survey data collected from 7,828 adults aged 65 and older between 1999 and 2016.
LONGER LIVES, WORSE HEALTH? SCIENTISTS UNCOVER TROUBLING TREND ACROSS GENERATIONS
Trained staff directly inspected participants' pill bottles to verify medication use over the previous 30 days, then followed them for an average of 8.5 years, according to a press release.
More than half of participants (54.3%) fell into at least one high-risk medication category. The largest group consisted of older adults taking five or more prescription drugs (polypharmacy).
Over 40% of older adults studied were taking five or more prescription medications, a situation known as polypharmacy. (iStock)
Another group, 37.6% of those studied, used medications deemed risky for older individuals, such as drugs that can increase the risk of confusion or falls, the study revealed.
Additionally, 11.4% took combinations of medications that are known to cause major drug-to-drug interactions.
DOCTORS REVEAL HIDDEN DANGER FOR SOME OZEMPIC, WEGOVY USERS WITH BRAIN DISORDERS

"People taking more medications often have more underlying health conditions, which may also contribute to their higher mortality risk," Katy Dubinsky, New York-based pharmacist and founder of PostGigs, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.

After accounting for overall health and underlying conditions, taking five or more prescriptions was associated with a 38% increase in overall mortality risk. Each additional prescription medication added to a patient’s routine was linked to a 7% increase in death risk.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Taking multiple medications has been shown to increase the likelihood of side effects, adverse drug reactions and accidental overdose, particularly as the liver and kidneys age and process drugs less efficiently, according to medical experts at Cleveland Clinic.
Researchers emphasized that these findings can help doctors identify patients who would benefit from safely stopping or reducing unnecessary medications. (iStock)

The total number of medications participants took was the strongest independent predictor of mortality, even after accounting for drug-to-drug interactions and potentially inappropriate prescriptions.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
These findings could help doctors determine which patients are the best candidates for "deprescribing," or carefully reducing or stopping unnecessary medications, the researchers stated.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The authors noted several limitations, including that the study focused strictly on community-dwelling older adults, excluding those living in nursing homes or assisted care facilities.

Additionally, medication use was documented during a single 30-day snapshot at the start of the study, meaning researchers could not track subsequent changes in prescriptions or evolving health conditions over time.
Because the study relied on a single 30-day snapshot of medication use, it shows an association rather than direct proof that the prescriptions caused the higher death risk. (iStock)
Experts emphasized that observational studies show association rather than direct causation.
"I would not recommend that anyone stop a medication because of this study," said Dubinsky.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Instead, she recommends that people taking multiple medications should periodically review everything they take with their physician or pharmacist, including prescriptions, over-the-counter medications, vitamins and supplements.
"Ask why each medication is being taken, whether it is still needed and whether the dose remains appropriate," Dubinsky advised.

title: Daily eating habit linked to better brain health in older adults, new research suggests
summary: A six-month trial found that older women who ate within eight to nine hours daily showed cognitive improvements beyond what weight loss alone provided.
story: Dr. Mary Claire Haver breaks down how the menopause shift rewires metabolism, raising abdominal fat and inflammation, and reveals why tracking strength and fat distribution beats relying on the number on the scale.
Eating within a shorter daily window could help support brain health as people age, according to new research.

Preliminary findings presented at NUTRITION 2026 — the American Society for Nutrition’s annual meeting in Maryland — suggests that older women who ate within eight to nine hours per day saw slight cognitive improvement compared to those who spread their meals over about 12 hours each day.
The small six-month trial included 47 postmenopausal obese or overweight women aged 50 to 79. They were each advised to reduce their daily food intake by about 500 calories.
INTERMITTENT FASTING'S REAL BENEFIT MAY COME AFTER YOU START EATING AGAIN
Study findings

The participants were divided into two groups. One ate in a time-restricted window within an average of 8.2 hours, usually from 10 a.m. to 6 p.m. The other group ate across a 12.3-hour window, according to a news release.
Both groups saw weight-loss results, but the shorter-window group scored higher on cognitive tests. (iStock)
Both groups lost about 15 pounds over six months, but those in the shorter eating-window group performed better on cognitive tests measuring spatial planning and problem-solving.
The shorter-window group also showed fewer errors on memory and learning tests, but no meaningful differences in reaction time or multi-tasking ability.
PEOPLE LOST WEIGHT WHILE EATING SIGNIFICANTLY MORE FOOD — HERE'S THE SECRET

"These outcomes suggest a better ability to remember information during everyday tasks and reduce mistakes related to memory, attention and problem-solving," lead researcher Sue Shapses, Ph.D., a professor at Rutgers University and Rutgers-RWJ Medical Center, said in a press release. "Reductions in the eating window predicted greater improvements."

Although the pilot study included only a small number of participants, the researchers believe that time-restricted eating may support brain health by regulating circadian rhythm, reducing inflammation and improving metabolic health.
"Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."
Losing weight alone can help "ward off some of the aging-related cognitive decline," according to Shapses.

"And these data suggest there may be additional benefits if you stop eating four hours prior to going to sleep and reduce food intake to eight to nine hours per day, compared to the usual eating window of 12 hours per day."
People who are overweight or obese tend to face a higher likelihood of developing dementia as they age, the researchers said. (iStock)
Women, as well as adults who are overweight or obese, tend to face a higher likelihood of developing Alzheimer’s disease and other forms of dementia as they age, according to the researchers.
How might meal timing help the brain?

Lauri Wright, Ph.D., director of nutrition programs and associate professor at the University of South Florida College of Public Health, who was not involved in this research, reflected on these findings in an interview with Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"This is an interesting study because it suggests that when we eat may matter in addition to what and how much we eat," she said. "That suggests meal timing itself may have played a role, not just weight loss."
"The results are promising, but we need larger, longer studies before recommending time-restricted eating specifically to improve brain health."
Brain imaging should be performed within the first several hours after seeking medical attention for a stroke, a doctor advised. (iStock)
Experts are still learning about how intermittent fasting affects the brain, although "several biological mechanisms are being considered," Wright noted.

"Giving the body a longer overnight break from eating may improve insulin sensitivity, reduce chronic inflammation, support healthy circadian rhythms and allow cells more time for repair and maintenance," she said. "Those processes are all linked to healthy brain aging."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

From a practical standpoint, eating within a shorter daily window often leads people to consume fewer calories, which can promote weight loss, according to New York-based certified holistic nutritionist Robin DeCicco.
"We know that maintaining a healthy weight helps with virtually everything," she told Fox News Digital. "Eating within a restricted window helps people cut calories."
"When you fast or... have periods of time where you're not just eating throughout the whole day, it does help to lower markers of inflammation and certain sources of oxidative stress."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Many people have reported "feeling better" when fasting, DeCicco noted — especially those who have inflammatory conditions, which can include neurological disorders like Alzheimer’s and dementia.
"When you're fasting, you're giving your organs a chance to rest, you're giving the digestive system a chance to ‘rest and digest,’" she added.
Fasting gives the organs a chance to "rest and digest," an expert said. (iStock)
Intermittent fasting isn’t the only way to support cognitive health, Wright countered.

"Regular physical activity, adequate sleep, controlling blood pressure and blood sugar, avoiding smoking, maintaining social connections and following an overall healthy dietary pattern, such as the Mediterranean diet, have much stronger evidence for protecting cognitive function over time," she said. "Think of meal timing as one potential piece of the puzzle rather than a magic bullet."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Intermittent fasting "isn’t appropriate for everyone," Wright warned, adding that she would advise against it for children and teens, pregnant or breastfeeding women, anyone with a history of an eating disorder, and people with diabetes who are taking insulin.
DeCicco agreed that fasting should be recommended and monitored by a medical professional, especially for those who take certain medications or have certain conditions.
Angelica Stabile is a lifestyle reporter for Fox News Digital.

title: Abdul El-Sayed’s Medicare-for-all crusade collides with an awkward contradiction involving his wife
summary: Abdul El-Sayed pushes Medicare-for-all, but his wife's psychiatry practice refuses all insurance, forcing patients to pay entirely out of pocket.
story: Zeteo host Mehdi Hasan pressed Michigan Democratic Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed about calling himself a ‘physician’ despite lacking a state medical license, asking whether he ‘told the truth.’
Michigan Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed has campaigned on passing Medicare-for-all, but his wife’s private psychiatry practice appears to operate outside the insurance system entirely.

El-Sayed, who secured the Democratic nomination for Senate on Wednesday, has argued that "healthcare shouldn't depend on who signs your paycheck" and demanded that taxpayers pay to "guarantee healthcare from cradle to grave" through Medicare-for-all. Despite this, his wife, Sarah Jukaku, states on her medical practice’s website that she is out of network with all insurance companies, generally requiring patients to pay the practice directly, though some may be eligible for out-of-network reimbursement.

Prior to July 2026, the FAQ section of Jukaku's website for her practice included the question "do you accept my insurance?" accompanied by the answer "no," according to The Washington Free Beacon. Her profile on Psychology Today, a popular professional database for therapists and psychiatrists, also at one point noted that she did not accept insurance.
Jukaku operates her own practice where she is the sole physician.
DR MARC SIEGEL: A SENATE CANDIDATE'S MEDICAL TITLE SPARKS A DEBATE VOTERS SHOULDN'T IGNORE
Abdul El-Sayed, candidate for U.S. Senate in Michigan, speaks before U.S. Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., takes the stage at Mumford High School on May 3, 2026, in Detroit. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

Amid media scrutiny in July, the practice’s website became inaccessible to the public and displayed a message indicating that it was private. Fox News Digital reached Jukaku and her practice multiple times via phone and email but received no response.

It is not rare for psychiatrists to turn away patients on Medicare. A 2022 analysis by KFF found that 40% of psychiatrists did not participate in Medicare, among the highest rate of any medical specialty.
Even as his wife's psychiatry practice reportedly operates on an out-of-network model, El-Sayed has repeatedly stressed the importance of expanding access to government-backed healthcare.

In a 2020 interview with the National Alliance on Mental Illness, for instance, he stated that "my wife's a psychiatrist, and we talk about the fact that a lot of folks don't do psychiatry because it's not as well recompensed as other practices simply because it's undervalued in the system." He went on to argue that the United States needs to build a "system" that "recognizes" the importance of treating "mental illness" due to the prevalence of "serious mental illness" and "death by suicide."
Years later, at a September 2025 campaign event, El-Sayed lamented that individuals with "serious mental illness" often "fall out of care" due to "transitions in health insurance."
MICHIGAN DEM SENATOR THROWS SUPPORT BEHIND CANDIDATE TO REPLACE HIM IN CONTENTIOUS PRIMARY
Abdul El-Sayed, a U.S. Senate candidate from Michigan, has been endorsed by Bernie Sanders and embraced comparisons between him and Zohran Mamdani. (Bill Pugliano/Getty Images)

The couple reported nearly $686,000 in total income in 2025, underscoring the contrast between El-Sayed's calls for expanded government-backed healthcare and his wife's out-of-network psychiatry practice.

The couple reported $686,069 in total income and $675,246 in adjusted gross income on two pages of their 2025 tax return released Wednesday. El-Sayed also sports a collection of luxury watches ranging in value from $2,000 to $10,000 apiece.
MICHIGAN SENATE HOPEFUL ABDUL EL-SAYED FIRES BACK AT CNN CHOOSING TO 'FIXATE' ON 'DEFUND THE POLICE' COMMENTS

Abdul El-Sayed answers a question during a news conference at the Michigan Democratic Party State Endorsement Convention in Detroit April 19, 2026, as communications director Roxie Richner looks on. (Jose Juarez/AP Photo)

"He regularly wears a SAR Rescue Timer on the campaign trail because he is trying to rescue our politics from corporate corruption," El-Sayed spokeswoman Roxie Richner told The Washington Free Beacon. "Sometimes he wears a vintage doctor's watch because he is a doctor."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Though El-Sayed earned a medical degree, he was never a licensed physician, which caused controversy amid allegations that he had claimed to be a practicing doctor.

"He has earned the right to be called ‘doctor’ twice over," a campaign spokesperson said at the time, alluding to the fact that he received both a medical degree and a doctorate degree in public health.
The El-Sayed campaign and Jukaku did not respond to requests for comment when reached by Fox News Digital.

title: Trump's antitrust point man could reshape Big Tech cases against Google and Apple if confirmed
summary: Adam Candeub's Senate confirmation hearing could reshape landmark antitrust cases against Google and Apple as he pushes for Section 230 reform.
story: Google General Counsel Halimah Delaine Prado joins 'Fox & Friends' to detail how Google is fighting AI-powered phishing scams.

President Donald Trump's pick to lead the Justice Department's Antitrust Division testified before the Senate on Wednesday in a confirmation hearing that could shape the future direction of the government's fight against Big Tech.

If confirmed, Adam Candeub, a longtime telecommunications law scholar and former Federal Communications Commission general counsel, would take control of some of the most consequential antitrust cases in decades, including the Justice Department’s landmark lawsuits targeting Google’s dominance in online search and Apple’s control over the App Store and its rules for developers.
The cases could determine how aggressively the government pursues antitrust cases against the country's largest technology companies.
FOX NEWS POLL: MOVE OVER BIG BROTHER, VOTERS SEE BIG TECH AS GREATER THREAT TO US
Google logos are seen in this photo illustration together with images of President Donald Trump. (Jaap Arriens/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
As head of the Antitrust Division, Candeub would oversee those cases and decide whether to continue the Justice Department's aggressive antitrust efforts against the largest technology companies.

Candeub has emerged as one of the conservative movement’s most prominent critics of Big Tech, arguing that dominant online platforms have accumulated too much power and that regulators have historically overlooked the larger impact of technology companies on competition, speech and public discourse.

"Big Tech’s market power undermines our nation’s culture of vibrant democratic deliberation," Candeub testified before Congress in March 2023. "Elon Musk’s Twitter files demonstrated that Big Tech has indeed limited particular groups, including dissenters, from important government policies from full participation in national political discussions.
"This power to exclude threatens all Americans," Candeub continued. "Power to silence one group of Americans will be used sooner or later to silence another."
META MEDICARE SCAM ADS TARGETING SENIORS FACE SCRUTINY
Attorney General Bill Barr holds a news conference at the Department of Justice, Dec. 21, 2020, in Washington, D.C. (Michael Reynolds-Pool/Getty Images)

Candeub has pushed for changes to Section 230, the federal law that protects online platforms from being held liable for much of the content posted by users. During Trump's first administration, he served at the National Telecommunications and Information Administration, where he helped lead efforts to narrow those legal protections for online platforms under Section 230.

And in his contribution to Project 2025, the conservative policy blueprint developed by the Heritage Foundation for a potential second Trump administration, Candeub argued that antitrust enforcement failed to account for the influence of major technology platforms over competition and the flow of information being shared.

"The large internet platforms have transformed the U.S. economy, streamlining consumer purchases, networking billions of people, and altering long-established business practices," Candeub wrote. "Despite their enormous size, they have avoided significant antitrust liability or prosecution. The reasons for this are not entirely clear."

Candeub’s nomination has drawn support from former Justice Department officials, including former Attorney General Bill Barr, who appointed Candeub as an associate deputy attorney general in 2020 during the first Trump administration.
TODD BLANCHE 'HONORED AND HUMBLED' BY TRUMP'S AG NOMINATION AFTER EXPLOSIVE WEEK OF FEDERAL ARRESTS
Barr praised Candeub’s expertise in telecommunications law and his academic background, describing him as a knowledgeable and capable leader for the Antitrust Division.
"I think he'll be a strong leader, and he's very knowledgeable," Barr told Fox News Digital. "I think he'll be balanced and fair and apply the law."

Barr is among more than a dozen current and former Justice Department officials who signed a letter to the Senate Judiciary Committee supporting Candeub’s nomination. The letter highlighted his experience at the FCC, the Office of the Associate Attorney General, the NTIA and his work as a law professor at Michigan State University.
INDIANA REPUBLICAN SENATOR MOVES TO BLOCK KIDS FROM ACCESSING PORN ONLINE

"Adam Candeub has the experience and the qualifications to live up to that storied legacy," the letter stated, arguing that the Antitrust Division’s next leader must be prepared to address the growing challenges posed by technology, social media and artificial intelligence.

"The Division’s next leader must be able to meet those questions with both intellectual seriousness and practical judgment," the letter continued. "Mr. Candeub is uniquely qualified to do so."

Sen. Dick Durbin, D-Ill., said on X that he recently met with Candeub to discuss issues including merger reviews, Section 230 reform and efforts to protect children online.

title: Fauci slapped with subpoena as COVID doc probed for 'profiting' off federal guidance
summary: The subpoena seeks documents on Anthony Fauci's book deals, awards and alleged self-dealing tied to COVID-19 guidance that impacted Florida businesses.
story: Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier joins John Roberts to discuss launching an investigation and sending a subpoena to Dr. Anthony Fauci. This development comes as a Senate panel prepares to vote on a contempt resolution after Fauci invoked the Fifth Amendment 111 times during recent Capitol Hill testimony regarding the origins of COVID-19.
FIRST ON FOX: A top Florida official is slapping Anthony Fauci with a subpoena over alleged "profiting" from federal guidance that hurt businesses, residents.
Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier announced Wednesday he has issued an investigative subpoena against former National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Disease Director Anthony Fauci.
The subpoena is part of a state probe into Fauci’s awards, incentives and guidance that impacted Florida’s residents and their businesses during the coronavirus pandemic.
FAUCI'S FIFTH FUELS VOW TO HAUL HIM INTO COURT 'EVERY DAY' DESPITE BIDEN PARDON
A split of Florida Attorney General James Uthmeier and former NIAID Director Anthony Fauci (Dominic Gwinn/Middle East Images/AFP via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

The announcement comes after Uthmeier, along with Sen. Tommy Tuberville, R-Ala., pledged to have Fauci investigated at the state level following his Senate Homeland Security and Government Affairs Committee hearing last week when he pleaded the Fifth 111 times and references were made to his blanket federal pardon from former President Joe Biden.

"We issued a formal subpoena to Dr. Fauci under Florida state law, seeking a breadth of documents ranging to what he knew when he knew it, his doubts about the safety and efficacy of vaccines that he's out there promoting, and we're really focused in on his self-dealing," Uthmeier announced on Fox News.

"Evidence has come to light that he was trying to personally profit off of this. This is outside of his government duties, his official role: He's trying to pursue book deals, awards, get connected with high rollers that might help him come into millions and millions of dollars. This is wrong, and it could go towards a deceptive trade practice, fraud, public nuisance, you name it. I think there's many aspects of Florida law that now are implicated."

Uthmeier said the activities he is being subpoenaed over were revealed largely through his diary – several hundred pages of writings made on a federal server that Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., released last week.
FAUCI'S NEWLY RELEASED COVID DIARIES REVEAL BIZARRE FIXATION ON FAME AS PANDEMIC DEATHS MOUNTED

Former NIH Director Anthony Fauci listens during a Senate Homeland Security and Governmental Affairs Committee hearing on July 29, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Fauci declined to answer questions, asserting his Fifth Amendment right. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)
"We know one award in particular, he made $900,000 on that," he said, appearing to refer to Fauci receiving approximately that amount from the Dan David Prize from Tel Aviv University.
Uthmeier said that when a bureaucrat is issuing directives and mandates he is privately questioning while also deriving a profit from that work, it raises legal questions.
"It starts as a civil inquiry," Uthmeier said. "But we're going to tie in all aspects of Florida common law, things ranging from deceptive trade, fraud, public nuisance, nothing is off the table."
The subpoena asks for awards Fauci applied to, considered or received from any organization, including those within the state of Florida, relating to the pandemic.
FAUCI PRIVATELY TOOK CREDIT FOR COVID-19 LOCKDOWNS DESPITE PUBLIC DENIAL, NEWLY EXPOSED DIARY ENTRIES REVEAL

Anthony Fauci declined to testify in a Senate committee hearing on his role in the US response to Covid-19, invoking his 5th Amendment rights. (Left (Alex WROBLEWSKI / AFP via Getty Images), Right (Al Drago/Bloomberg via Getty Images))

It also asks for information on professional opportunities offered to or considered by Fauci, as well as interactions and communications with Florida businesses, media outlets and communities regarding COVID-19 vaccination sites, social distancing and mask orders, and school closures.
A pair of other states expressed encouragement at the news.
West Virginia Attorney General JB McCuskey alleged Fauci’s refusal to answer Paul’s questions is "concerning" and that the American people deserve to know whether they were misled or "manipulated."
"Both my Office and I support Attorney General Uthmeier’s efforts to uncover the truth," McCuskey said in a statement obtained by Fox News Digital.
Louisiana Attorney General Liz Murrill added that the public "deserves answers to about a million questions related to the pandemic, its origins, and the government’s actions in response."
Murrill alleged Fauci had lied and said that "we just don’t know how much" so.
"But he lied about something as basic as keeping a diary. The truth will come out."

title: SEE IT: Michigan Dem predicts far-left El-Sayed will win Senate race after backing his primary rival
summary: Sen. Gary Peters says Abdul El-Sayed will beat Mike Rogers in the Michigan Senate race despite backing Haley Stevens in the Democratic primary.
story: Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., told Fox News Digital that Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed will beat Republican nominee Mike Rogers in November's midterms, despite backing Democratic rival as successor. (Credit: Fox News Digital)

Sen. Gary Peters, D-Mich., is confident that far-left Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed will defeat Republican nominee Mike Rogers in the race to replace him in the Senate, despite having endorsed El-Sayed’s primary rival, Rep. Haley Stevens.

El-Sayed, known as a progressive insurgent, will go head-to-head with Michigan’s Republican Senate nominee Mike Rogers in the upcoming midterm elections. El-Sayed’s victory marks yet another win for the left-wing Democrats in this year’s primaries that have been battling to defeat the current Democratic establishment.

"I think if you look at the issues broadly, the differences between Abdul El-Sayed and Rogers when it comes to fighting for families in Michigan, it's pretty broad," Peters said to Fox News Digital when asked if his far-left positions could give Republicans a boost in Michigan.
2026 MIDTERMS STATE OF PLAY: KEY RACES UNFOLD AS STEVENS, EL-SAYED BATTLE IN MICHIGAN

Abdul El-Sayed, a progressive candidate in the Democratic primary for U.S. Senate in Michigan, films a social media video at a pool party for content creators supporting his campaign, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, in Detroit. (AP Photo/Julia Demaree Nikhinson)
He continued, "And in the end, that's why he will prevail."

Peters’ endorsement of Stevens over El-Sayed was part of a broader effort by mainstream Democrats to beat another progressive candidate, as Republicans largely viewed El-Sayed winning as a boost for their party’s chances to flip Michigan’s Senate seat. Rogers told Fox News Digital in an interview prior to the primary results that he would "beat either one of those candidates," but that El-Sayed has "his own special sauce of crazy."

The race between Stevens and El-Sayed was strenuous as it became a determining factor of whether Democrats could win the majority back in the Senate. More than $80 million was poured into this primary, qualifying it as the most expensive Democratic Senate nomination race in history.
DEMS' LEFTWARD LURCH GETS LEGS AS EL-SAYED'S MICHIGAN SENATE VICTORY SPARKS PARTY DEBATE
Rep. Haley Stevens and former public health official Abdul El-Sayed competed for the Democratic nomination for U.S. Senate in Michigan. (Scott Olson/Getty Images; Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Republicans have speculated that the turn to nominating Democratic socialist candidates indicates that the current Democratic establishment is losing its grip in these congressional races.
Peters pushed back on this claim, arguing that the results aren’t reflective of the entire party as this is "nothing new" for the state.

"Michigan is a very diverse state, and if you recall, Bernie Sanders beat Hillary Clinton many years ago in a primary in Michigan, so this is nothing new," Peters said, referring to the state's 2016 Democratic presidential primary.
Sanders, I-Vt., endorsed El-Sayed in his Senate primary to defeat Stevens.
HASAN PIKER UNLOADS ON 'ISLAMOPHOBIC PIECES OF S---' DEMOCRATS AS EL-SAYED FACES PARTY UNITY TEST

Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, Michigan Democratic U.S. Senate primary candidate Abdul El-Sayed and Sen. Bernie Sanders greet the crowd during a campaign rally on July 18, 2026, in Detroit. (Sarah Rice/Getty Images)

El-Sayed, a former Wayne County Health Department director, would be the first Muslim senator. He has called for defunding the police and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE). He is also a strong critic of Israel, labeling the country’s actions as genocide against Palestinians in Gaza.
Peters declined to weigh in on where he falls on El-Sayed's policy positions — like defunding the police — despite expressing confidence the Democratic nominee will defeat Rogers.
"I'm not on the ballot, so I don't have to make those kinds of statements," Peters said.

title: Senate confirms new CDC director as diarrhea-causing parasite outbreak sweeps US
summary: Dr. Erica Schwartz was confirmed as CDC director along party lines amid concerns over whether she would stand up to Robert F. Kennedy Jr. on vaccines.
story: CNN's Dana Bash sparred with HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy, Jr. over vaccine efficacy amid rising measles cases in the U.S. on "State of the Union" Sunday.

The Senate confirmed the next director of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) as viral outbreaks wreak havoc across the country, and as lawmakers worry whether they’ve found someone to stand up to President Donald Trump’s top health official.

The upper chamber confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to be the next CDC director on Wednesday along party lines. Her confirmation comes as a Cyclospora outbreak, commonly known as the diarrhea parasite, carves its way across the U.S. from contaminated lettuce.
Schwartz is the latest person to lead the agency during Trump’s second term in a position that has seen nearly a half dozen different names and faces helming the nation’s disease-fighting outfit.
CYCLOSPORA OUTBREAK: IS IT STILL SAFE TO EAT AT RESTAURANTS? HERE'S WHAT TO KNOW
The Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to be the next director of the Centers for Disease Control. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
She almost didn’t make the cut for a full confirmation vote.

Lawmakers on the Senate Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) Committee grilled Schwartz on whether she would actually stand up to the Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and his position on vaccines.

Notably, HELP Committee Chair Bill Cassidy, R-La., who proved the decisive vote to confirm Kennedy last year, didn’t buy whether she would just take orders or make scientific and medically-based decisions.
TRUMP BLASTS SEN BILL CASSIDY AS ‘DISLOYAL DISASTER,’ PUSHES CHALLENGER JULIA LETLOW IN LOUISIANA GOP PRIMARY
When pressed during her initial committee hearing whether she would buck orders that were politically motivated, Schwartz told Cassidy, "The secretary will absolutely allow me to be CDC director."

"I feel like I’m having to go after this question a little bit more firmly than I feel like I should," Cassidy said. "You can be CDC director and just take orders. We need a CDC director that will actually stand up to crazy, stupid things being said that undermine faith in immunization."

That changed, though, and Schwartz cleared her committee test. Cassidy, who has used his newfound freedom to test the waters against the administration after being ousted by a Trump-backed opponent in his primary, said the agency "needs someone who understands that the way to prevent vaccine-preventable diseases is to reassure the public that vaccines are safe and effective."
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK SPARKS BACKLASH, SPLITS MAHA MOVEMENT
A massive surge in Cyclospora cases means people may be mistaking this parasitic foodborne infection for a standard summer stomach bug. (iStock)
"I’m confident that she knows what she is doing and will stand against those who do not," he said.
Schwartz, who served as deputy surgeon general during Trump’s first term, is not the first CDC director to be confirmed during this Congress.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The first was Susan Monarez, who lasted only a month in the role.
Monarez received glowing praise from Trump during her confirmation process, but was swiftly booted from the position over what appeared to be a disagreement with Kennedy over vaccines.
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Dem drops US Senate bid, leaving independent candidate as lone challenger to incumbent GOP Sen Mike Rounds
summary: Democratic Senate candidate Julian Beaudion dropped out of the South Dakota race, leaving only GOP Sen. Mike Rounds and independent challenger Brian Bengs in the contest.
story: Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., commemorates the life and legacy of his colleague Lindsey Graham, sharing personal anecdotes from their time together at the NATO summit.

Julian Beaudion, the Democratic candidate who was challenging Republican Sen. Mike Rounds of South Dakota, announced he is dropping his election bid, a move that leaves independent candidate Brian Bengs going head-to-head against the incumbent lawmaker.

"As many of you know, we experienced a devastating house fire while continuing to navigate significant personal financial hardship," Beaudion explained in part of a lengthy statement issued Tuesday. "Through it all, my wife, Inkka, and our daughters have shown incredible strength. They have sacrificed more than anyone should ever be asked to sacrifice for a campaign. Today, my first responsibility is to them.
"After the fire, an opponent and those associated with the opponent, hit my family and I with intimidating threats to drop out of this race,' he said in the statement.

"Those attacks were personal and never about politics. The mental and physical safety of my family is my priority and for this reason alone, I step aside. This is a time for my family to heal and for South Dakota voters to choose a Senator. Not a time for me to talk of specific threats and attacks. But rest assured that time will come."
GOP GOVERNOR SURVIVES CHALLENGE FROM BITCOIN EVANGELIST IN GUBERNATORIAL RUNOFF

U.S. Senate candidate Julian Beaudion speaks during the McGovern Day Dinner hosted by the Democratic Party June 5, 2026, at the Ramkota Exhibit Hall in Sioux Falls, S.D. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)
Beaudion said he will not back either of the remaining candidates in the contest.
"Let me be clear, I will not be endorsing or supporting Brian Bengs in this race," he noted. "Likewise, I cannot support Senator Mike Rounds."
TRUMP ENDORSES GOP SENATOR YEARS AFTER ASSERTING 'I WILL NEVER ENDORSE THIS JERK AGAIN'
Sen. Mike Rounds, R-S.D., during votes in the U.S. Capitol June 17, 2026. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

South Dakota Democratic Party Chair Shane Merrill said in a statement, "Julian would have made an outstanding U.S. Senator for South Dakota."
REPUBLICAN WHO REPORTEDLY DROPPED OUT DEFEATS TRUMP'S PICK IN KEY SWING-DISTRICT PRIMARY
U.S. Senate candidate Brian Bengs speaks during a Democratic rally Nov. 7, 2022, at the Washington Pavilion in Sioux Falls. (USA Today Network via Reuters Connect)

"Every city, town, and reservation he's visited, people truly felt like they were being heard. Julian is the kind of leader we need in Congress. He is fair, understanding and open minded. Thank you Julian for your dedication to the people of South Dakota," Merrill noted.

title: El-Sayed campaign backed by over $100,000 from dozens of members of group with alleged terror ties
summary: Abdul El-Sayed's Senate campaign collected over $115,000 from CAIR officials and leaders, including an executive who praised Hamas on Oct. 7.
story: Rep. Chip Roy, R-Texas, discusses Gov. Greg Abbott’s decision to declare CAIR and the Muslim Brotherhood as a terrorist organization and investigations into Sharia courts in the Lone Star State on ‘The Will Cain Show.’

FIRST ON FOX: GRAND RAPIDS, MI - Michigan Democratic Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed's campaign has collected more than $115,000 from individuals who work for or have held leadership roles with the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR), which has been designated a terrorist organization by the United Arab Emirates and formally designated or labeled as such in Florida and Texas.

A Fox News Digital review found that El-Sayed, who has made getting "money out of politics" a central campaign rallying cry, has accepted donations from at least 41 individuals who either work for CAIR, formerly worked for CAIR, or have served in leadership positions with the organization.

The donor list includes several of CAIR's highest-ranking officials, including national Board Chair Manal Fakhoury, national Board Treasurer Eyas Abdeen, national Vice Chair Emad Sabbah, and CAIR-Michigan board member Jukaku Tayeb, El-Sayed's father-in-law.

Tayeb has been one of the largest financial backers of the super PAC supporting El-Sayed's campaign and is also part of the founding committee of the Islamic Society of North America (ISNA), a group linked to Hamas and Muslim Brotherhood funding, Washington Free Beacon first reported.
DEMS CLASH OVER AIPAC MONEY, ‘OGRE’ ATTACK AND ELECTABILITY DURING CRUCIAL SENATE DEBATE

Abdul El-Sayed speaks during a Democratic primary election-night event in his race against Haley Stevens on Wednesday, Aug. 5, 2026, at the Majestic Theatre in Detroit. (Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP Photo)

One donor, CAIR Executive Director Nihad Awad, listed in FEC records under the name Nehad Hammad, drew national condemnation after saying he was "happy" to see Hamas break out of Gaza on Oct. 7, 2023, and arguing Israel "does not have the right to self-defense" as an occupying power.

The contributions were not limited to Michigan. Fox News Digital identified donations from CAIR national leaders and officials affiliated with chapters in California, Arizona, Texas, Georgia, Washington, Illinois, Minnesota and Ohio, among other states, illustrating the breadth of support El-Sayed received from within the organization's leadership ranks.

Other names on the donor list include CAIR-California Governance Board Treasurer Rubina Alvi, CAIR-California Governance Board Chair Asaad Traina, CAIR-Michigan board member Muzammil Ahmed, who contributed $11,600 to El-Sayed's campaign, CAIR-California Governance Board member Atef Ibrahim, CAIR-California Governance Board member Dina Ezzeddine, and former CAIR National Board Chair Roula Allouch.
EL-SAYED PALS AROUND WITH FAR-LEFT STREAMER HASAN PIKER THE DAY BEFORE CRUCIAL MICHIGAN SENATE ELECTION
Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed poses for a portrait in Grand Rapids, Michigan, on Saturday, Feb. 21, 2026. (Evan Cobb for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

El-Sayed has maintained ties to CAIR beyond campaign fundraising. In 2022, he appeared at a CAIR event and was paid for a speaking engagement, where he criticized Oklahoma's ban on Sharia law and compared it to the Trail of Tears, Washington Free Beacon reported.

CAIR has long been the subject of controversy over its alleged ties to Hamas. In 2007, federal prosecutors named the organization an unindicted co-conspirator in the Holy Land Foundation terrorism financing case, the largest terrorism financing prosecution in U.S. history.

Although CAIR was never charged with a crime, federal prosecutors argued the organization was part of a network created to support Hamas in the United States. CAIR has denied the allegations and has challenged its inclusion as an unindicted co-conspirator.

In recent years, Florida and Texas have formally designated or labeled CAIR a terrorist organization, while the United Arab Emirates designated the group a terrorist organization in 2014 which is widely understood to stem from the UAE's view that CAIR has ties to the Muslim Brotherhood.

In response to Fox News Digital's request for comment, CAIR denied allegations that it has ties to terrorism, citing its "Dispelling Rumors About CAIR" webpage, a memorandum stating it has "repeatedly condemned antisemitism throughout our 30 years of existence" and "for decades" condemned terrorist attacks by Hamas and other designated terrorist groups, as well as a 2009 statement saying, "We unequivocally condemn all acts of terrorism, whether carried out by al-Qa’ida, the Real IRA, FARC, Hamas, ETA, or any other group designated by the U.S. Department of State as a ‘Foreign Terrorist Organization."CAIR also cited a National Board statement condemning antisemitism and the Oct. 7, 2023, attacks, and a 2023 editorial in which National Executive Director Nihad Awad said he agreed with the organization's condemnation of attacks on civilians.
Fox News Digital reached out to the El-Sayed campaign for comment.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Hussam Ayloush, an executive director of CAIR, speaks during a press conference. (Marc Martin/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)

El-Sayed has repeatedly drawn criticism from Republicans and pro-Israel advocates over his associations and comments related to the Middle East, including campaigning with far-left streamer Hasan Piker, his response to an attack targeting a Detroit synagogue, and declining to comment on the death of Iran's supreme leader, citing constituents in Dearborn who were mourning.

El-Sayed defeated Dem. Rep. Haley Stevens in the Democratic Senate primary on Tuesday night in a race that was much closer than most pundits expected. El-Sayed will face off against Republican Mike Rogers, a former congressman, in November.

title: Schumer claims victory as Senate moves to avert shutdown; GOP says he got played
summary: The Senate advanced a continuing resolution unanimously, but Republicans and Democrats clashed over whether the deal blocks Trump's federal grants rule.
story: Tensions rise in Washington over a potential government shutdown by Oct. 1.
The Senate quietly moved its solution to halt a government shutdown through another key step as the tenuous truce between Republicans and Democrats continues to hold.
In the midst of a hectic, albeit open-ended and uncertainty-laden schedule, the upper chamber advanced its continuing resolution (CR) unanimously on Wednesday.
While not the final vote, it’s a strong sign that neither side wants to thrust the federal government into uncertainty as the midterms near.

It marks a sharp departure from the shutdown politics of the last year and follows Senate Republicans' hand-wringing for months that Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., would once again lead his caucus to the brink and shut the government down for political gain.
DEMOCRATS BLINK AS SCHUMER HELPS GOP CLEAR KEY SHUTDOWN HURDLE

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., speaks during a news conference after Senate Democratic policy luncheons at the U.S. Capitol in Washington, D.C., June 23, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
For now, that’s not happening.
And Schumer is saying that Democrats have wanted to keep the lights on in a bipartisan manner all along.

He contended that the CR, negotiated between the top Republican and Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, was a major victory for Democrats, particularly for its design to "stave off Trump's disgraceful effort to withhold federal grants from vital projects."

"I mean, what kind of country is this? You have two identical projects, one in a red state and one in a blue state funded the same way, same clean record," Schumer said. "He cancels the blue state one and says the red state one is OK."
TRUMP ADMIN PAUSING OVER $1B IN MEDICAID PAYMENTS TO MINNESOTA, CALIFORNIA OVER FRAUD, COMPLIANCE CONCERNS

The Office of Management and Budget (OMB) and the Trump administration are pushing for more control over federal grants, which critics like Schumer and others warn could be used as a political cudgel to dictate which states do and don’t get a flow of federal dollars.
If the CR passes and is signed by Trump, it will pause that rule change until Dec. 11, when the stopgap expires.
But Republicans say it’s not quite the victory Schumer thinks it is.
BOMB-THROWER DEM MAKES SHOCKING PROMISE TO KICK SCHUMER TO CURB DURING SENATE DEBATE

Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., is urging the Senate to craft the SAVE America Act into a budget reconciliation bill passable by a simple majority instead of the 60-vote filibuster. (Anna Moneymaker/Pool/AFP)
Sen. John Kennedy, R-La., countered that Schumer may think he won with the deal, but, in reality, it just delayed the inevitable for the White House’s plans for grant-funded projects.

"I think he's going to go back to his base and say, ‘I got the OMB rule killed,’" Kennedy said. "Well, he didn’t. I mean, I've talked to [OMB Director] Russ Vought, and the president this morning about that, and the rule can be ready by Dec. 11. So, no harm, no foul."
Alex Miller is a writer for Fox News Digital covering the U.S. Senate.

title: Tlaib moves to block ICE airport arrests, says TSA helping target immigrants
summary: Rashida Tlaib's bill would block ICE and Border Patrol from accessing TSA passenger screening data, travel records and data broker information.
story: The House floor was thrown into chaos on Wednesday after Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, accused Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., of Hezbollah ties while debating a Lebanon war powers resolution. (Credit: House of Representatives)

Progressive Democrats are taking their war against President Donald Trump's handling of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) to the skies with a new effort led by far-left Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich.

Tlaib introduced a bill on Tuesday aimed at blocking ICE and Border Patrol agents from accessing air travelers' data called the No TSA Data for ICE Act, which would curb federal immigration officials' ability to arrest noncitizens at U.S. airports.

The legislation would stop ICE and Customs and Border Protection (CBP) from being able to use data gathered by the Transportation Security Administration (TSA), which includes passenger screening records, travel records and personally identifiable passenger information purchased from private data brokers.

A TSA spokesperson ripped into Tlaib in response and argued the bill would make the U.S. vulnerable to terror threats. "As we approach the 25th anniversary of the horrific terror attacks of 9/11, it’s not shocking that some in the Democrat Party would want to neuter the Department of Homeland Security’s ability to protect Americans from terrorists," the spokesperson said.
DEMOCRAT COMPARES ICE TO 'DOMESTIC TERRORISTS' AS 111 HOUSE DEMS DEMAND TEXAS DETENTION CENTER CLOSE

Rep. Rashida Tlaib, D-Mich., is introducing a new bill aimed at blocking ICE and CBP from getting data from the TSA for immigration enforcement. (Paul Morigi/Getty Images for MomsRising; Patrick T. Fallon/AFP via Getty Images)
"DHS was established to prevent information silos that could create blind spots against threats. Does Rep. Tlaib want our enemies to be empowered to attack the U.S. again?" the TSA spokesperson said.

The bill would also block the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) from barring an individual from trusted traveler programs like TSA PreCheck based on their First Amendment-protected activity, like attending protests or speaking out against the administration.
Tlaib's bill has little chance of getting a vote in the current Republican-controlled Congress.
If enacted, it could significantly curb the ability of DHS' separate entities to coordinate immigration enforcement.
The Transportation Security Administration building on Feb. 13, 2026, in Springfield, Va. (Heather Diehl/Getty Images)
The Michigan Democrat said in a statement that the TSA was "complicit in ICE expanding its chaos and cruelty to target our communities in our airports."
HARRIS CALLS FOR ICE PROBE AFTER MAINE SHOOTING AMID RENEWED 'BORDER CZAR' CRITICISM

"Through an information-sharing agreement signed in 2025, TSA is readily offering up our immigrant residents to suffer at the hands of ICE agents so they can fulfill their daily arrest quota. One source from ICE even said it makes for ‘easy targets’ at airports—a disgusting exploitation of immigrants in status limbo," Tlaib said. "Immigrants should be able to safely fly in this country without the fear of arrest or deportation."
Democrats have near-universally hammered the Trump administration's immigration crackdown since the president came back to the White House in January 2025.

The criticism fueled the longest partial government shutdown in history, with DHS going unfunded for 76 days as Democrats protested federal immigration agents' killing of two U.S. citizens earlier this year — which also drew ire from Republicans.

title: Exclusive: Grieving mom reveals deadly cost of illegal immigration as daughter's killer seeks parole
summary: Angel Mom Kathy Hall recounts the night an illegal immigrant's speeding truck killed her 18-year-old daughter Hailey King in Fayetteville, Arkansas.
story: GRAPHIC CONTENT WARNING

FIRST ON FOX: After her 18-year-old daughter, Hailey King, was run over by an illegal immigrant driving a truck 36 mph above the speed limit, Angel Mom Kathy Hall promised her dying daughter she was "never going to stop fighting for justice for her."

In an interview obtained exclusively by Fox News Digital from advocacy group The American Border Story, Hall recounted her daughter’s grisly killing, which, she said, launched her crusade to make sure that no other parents and children undergo the same fate.

While riding a scooter with a friend in Fayetteville, Arkansas, King was hit from behind by a speeding truck driven by illegal alien Sergio Rodriguez. According to Hall, her daughter was on her way home for dinner. Upon impact, King was thrown onto the hood of the truck. Hall said Rodriguez continued driving, swerving into another lane and sending King headfirst onto the street. King suffered a brain stem hemorrhage, inner and outer cranial hemorrhages, a burst spleen and a lacerated liver. She died shortly after the Nov. 7, 2016, incident, leaving behind her 2-year-old daughter, Brooklyn.

Hall said Rodriguez was sentenced to 17 years in prison for manslaughter, battery and leaving the scene of a crime. After just one and a half years, Hall said she was notified that Rodriguez had become eligible for parole, forcing her to repeatedly relive her trauma each time she goes to court to testify against his release.
EXCLUSIVE: DHS HONORS ANGEL FAMILIES DURING NATIONAL CRIME VICTIMS WEEK, CALLS CRIMES 'COMPLETELY PREVENTABLE'

Hailey King (pictured) died at age 18 in November 2016 after she was ran over by illegal immigrant Sergio Rodriguez in a hit-and-run incident in Fayettville, Arkansas. (Courtesy of The American Border Story)
Hall said that authorities showed up at her door the night of the incident and told her, "You need to come with us to the hospital."
She said they took her to her daughter’s hospital room where she found her "sitting up at a kind of an angle and her eyes were wide open. But she was like staring off into space."

"I knew right when I looked at her that she was gone," said Hall. "So, I sat down with her and talked to her and told her how much I love her. Told her I was never going to stop fighting for justice for her… and then her heart stopped."

Besides King, Hall said that her daughter’s friend, Osmin "David" Gutierrez, was "trapped underneath the truck for over a mile" as the illegal immigrant continued driving. She said that "when sparks started happening, [Rodriguez] pulled into an apartment complex. And when he did, David's torso was – his legs detached, [and he] was left in the driveway screaming for his life."
"He was still conscious," she said.
Gutierrez died two years later from a blood clot resulting from his lost legs.
FAMILY SHATTERED AFTER 3-TIME DEPORTED ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT ALLEGEDLY BLEW THROUGH STOP SIGN, ROILING HOUSE RACE
Left: Hailey King and her siblings, left to right: Shawntay, Hailey, James and Nickolas. Right: Hailey, left, and her mother, Kathy Hall, right. (Courtesy of The American Border Story)

Despite her promise, Hall said getting justice for her daughter has been a "hard long road." After the incident, Hall said Rodriguez "disappeared for three days" before police found him. When he was apprehended, Hall said Rodriguez was released on bond in less than an hour.
She believes that Rodriguez was "protected every step of the way" during the trial process while she and her family "were treated like we were the criminals when we'd go into court."

Despite his immigration status, Hall said a decision was made not to notify U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement. She said she was told that "if we would have informed ICE that he was here and he was illegal, that they would have just picked him up and taken him down to Texas and sent him back and he would have never had to deal with the death of [her] daughter."
At the time, Hall said the family felt this "was kind of putting us in a rock and a hard place."

"It's so confusing to be there and say, ‘OK, do I want him to be deported right now or do I just want him to spend time either way and get him out?’" she said. "We had no idea, you know, a choice like that. What kind of decision do you make?"
'SLAP ON THE WRIST': ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT TRUCKER'S SENTENCE IGNITES OUTRAGE AFTER CRASH KILLED 3
Angel Mother Kathy Hall looks on at the gravesite of her daughter Hailey King, who was killed in 2016 at age 18 by an illegal immigrant. (Courtesy of The American Border Story)
Due to parole hearings, Hall said that she and her family "have to relive this right now every two years."

"As soon as the pain dulls a little bit, you have to go back through the whole thing preparing to try to keep him behind bars again," she said. "My daughter, the only thing she did wrong that day was being on the back of a scooter coming home for dinner. She didn't deserve this."

"She doesn't deserve for her daughter to not know who she is and how much she loved her. She doesn't deserve any of it, and she deserves to have the justice I promised to her as she was dying," Hall continued, concluding, "I'll never stop fighting; I'm going to do everything I can to keep my promise to her."

Peter Pinedo is a politics writer for Fox News Digital.

title: Controversial socialist chef flip-flops on abolish the police, says she’s ‘serious about public safety’
summary: Francesca Hong now says she is "serious about public safety" after previously calling to defund and abolish the police in her 2020 tweets.
story: Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong defends her past controversial social media posts during an interview on 'America's Newsroom.' Dana Perino grills the Democratic socialist candidate on her calls to defund the police, abolish the Senate, and eliminate ICE. Hong argues the comments require context and emphasizes her commitment to supporting working-class families across Wisconsin.

Controversial chef and democratic socialist candidate Francesca Hong has reversed her position on defunding and abolishing the police, saying in a recent podcast interview that she has become "serious about public safety."

Hong is a Wisconsin Democratic lawmaker perhaps best known for her 2020 call to "cancel Thanksgiving" because of its colonial history. She is a member of the Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) and a leading Democratic candidate for Wisconsin governor.

In an episode of "Pod Save America" released on Tuesday, Hong was asked about her 2020 tweets in which she wrote that "police exist to uphold white supremacy" and "I support defunding the police as a first step towards abolishing the police." The podcast host asked her, "I’m wondering how your views on policing have evolved since 2020?"
In response, Hong said, "My views have only become stronger in that I’m serious about public safety and I will not abolish the police."
SOCIALIST FRANCESCA HONG STRUGGLES TO EXPLAIN CALL TO 'CANCEL THANKSGIVING' AS POST RESURFACES

Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong listens to Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speak before being introduced during a campaign rally on Aug. 2, 2026, in Milwaukee. Hong, a democratic socialist in the state legislature, has seen an uptick in recent poll numbers. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

"My views are that people are struggling right now and need basic needs met, and I want to focus on stopping violent crime and giving law enforcement the resources and the training that they need, but ensure we are also holding accountable law enforcement that does not follow the law," she added.
Pressed on whether she still believes police exist to uphold White supremacy, Hong answered quickly, "No."
Hong was then asked, "What has changed in your thinking since you posted that in 2020?"

She answered, "I’ve had more conversations with people who are more directly connected to the problems and have learned that it is most important for a public servant like myself to make sure we’re looking at sensible, practical solutions that will help keep communities safe."
LEFT’S LATEST SOCIALIST DARLING DRAGGED OVER ‘WHITENESS’ COMMENTS PULLING IN HER OWN FAMILY: ‘WEIRDO RACISM’

Rep. Ilhan Omar and influencer and left-wing political commentator Hasan Piker stand with Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong during a campaign rally for Hong on Aug. 2, 2026. (Joshua Lott/Getty Images)

"When you talk to people who are most justice impacted, a mother who lost a child to police violence, people who have contended with injustices in historically marginalized communities, but just also looks like making sure we are implementing solutions and helping change the material conditions of people’s lives," she said.
During the interview, Hong also characterized her previous statement fantasizing about a "world without prisons" as "more aspirational."
Critics have argued that Hong has a history of expressing controversial progressive takes, with former X posts resurfacing in recent weeks.

In 2019, she wrote, "I ate two bites of my kid’s cheeseburger at a Culver’s in black river falls and told him they ran out of ice cream. Mostly just wanted to leave bc I was on the verge of a [sic] anxiety attack… to [sic] many old white people who didn’t think we spoke English."
DEMOCRATS' SHARP LEFT TURN? DSA'S INFLUENCE GROWS AS MIDTERMS, 2028 RACES TAKES SHAPE
Wisconsin gubernatorial candidate Francesca Hong. (Matthew Ludak for The Washington Post via Getty Images)

In another since-deleted post, Hong wrote, "Cancel Thanksgiving. Should have done this in 1621. If it takes a worldwide pandemic for us to realize we should stop celebrating colonialism and the original superspreader event that killed indigenous folx [sic] and women, so be it."
In a recent CNN appearance, Hong was asked, "Do you still believe that Thanksgiving should be canceled?"

title: White House pushes 'watershed' fraud-fighting reform in Congress as Vance convenes task force
summary: Vice President JD Vance participated in an anti-fraud task force roundtable event on Wednesday, proposing reforms to help crackdown on fraud.
story: Vice President JD Vance and White House aide Stephen Miller spoke at a Task Force to Eliminate Fraud roundtable event with lawmakers on Wednesday.
Vice President JD Vance, who chairs President Donald Trump's Task Force To Eliminate Fraud, said during remarks on Wednesday that the effort has identified $230 billion of suspected fraud so far.

"We've been able to stop $56 billion in fraudulent payments that would've otherwise gone to fraudsters, rather than to the people who need them," he said at a task-force roundtable event with lawmakers.
Vance called for reforms to help tackle the fraud.
VANCE TO HOST CONGRESS AT WHITE HOUSE TO DISCUSS LEGISLATIVE ACTION ON FRAUD

Vice President JD Vance speaks during a congressional roundtable on anti-fraud initiatives in the Indian Treaty Room of the Eisenhower Executive Office Building in Washington, D.C., on Aug. 5, 2026. (Mandel NGAN / AFP via Getty Images)

He said when the federal government distributes money to states for the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program (SNAP), the federal government has "no visibility into who is ultimately getting those benefits."

He said that if California provides "those food stamp benefits to an illegal alien, to a violent criminal, the federal government has no visibility, and sometimes the states themselves have no visibility."
"So we need to work with Congress, and we need some legislation that would actually force some data sharing between the state governments and the federal governments," the vice president said.
TOP FEDERAL PROSECUTOR CALLS CALIFORNIA A 'FRAUDSTER'S PARADISE,' WARNS STATE OFFICIALS COULD FACE CHARGES
Vice President JD Vance looks on during a Cabinet meeting at Camp David in Maryland, on July 31, 2026. (Aaron Schwartz / AFP via Getty Images)
Vance also floated the idea of tougher sentencing against those convicted of fraud.

White House deputy chief of staff for policy and Homeland Security advisor Stephen Miller called for "strict, clear, mandatory minimums" for fraudsters, saying they should be slapped with "a very substantial prison sentence."
DOJ CHARGES 19 DEFENDANTS IN ALLEGED $4M PHILADELPHIA MEDICARE AND MEDICAID FRAUD

"That change alone would be watershed for fighting fraud because it would mean that the Department of Justice would be able to, through prosecuting a few hundred or thousand cases in a year, be able to chill the criminal conduct of millions," Miller said.

title: Republican who reportedly dropped out defeats Trump's pick in key swing-district primary
summary: Trump-endorsed Amir Hassan lost the Republican primary in Michigan's 8th District to Thomas J. Smith, who will now face Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet.
story: FOX Business anchor David Asman and Fox News contributor Karl Rove discuss Michigan's Democratic U.S. Senate primary between Abdul El-Sayed and Rep. Haley Stevens as President Donald Trump delivers remarks at General Motors in Milford, Michigan, on ‘The Story.’

Republican voters in Michigan's 8th Congressional District chose Thomas J. Smith as their challenger to freshman Democratic Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet on Wednesday – defying President Donald Trump's endorsement of opponent Amir Hassan – in one of several House races the GOP hopes will help expand its majority in November.
The district stretches across Flint, Saginaw, Midland and Bay City, and has become increasingly competitive in recent election cycles. Al Lemmo also vied for the nomination.
Smith was a longtime GM employee, according to his website.
"We need strong conservative leadership that protects our constitutional freedoms, supports working families, secures our borders, and restores accountability in Washington," he said on his website.
TRUMP-BACKED FIREBRAND WINS ARIZONA GOP GOVERNOR PRIMARY, SETTING UP HIGH-STAKES SHOWDOWN
Rep. Kristen McDonald Rivet.
Smith reportedly suspended his campaign in July and endorsed Lemmo, according to the Detroit News, while Trump endorsed Hassan and invited him onstage at a recent rally.

Hassan spoke then about how many members of his family worked for GM. "The contrast is clear, the time is now," Hassan said. "Protecting America, getting back to the fundamentals… that’s what we’re doing this cycle."
HOUSE REPUBLICANS AIM TO TURN DEMOCRATIC CIVIL WAR INTO MIDTERM WEAPON
Thomas Smith won his congressional primary in Michigan (Credit: Tom Smith for Congress)

DEMOCRATS TARGET MORE GOP HOUSE SEATS AFTER SOCIALIST VICTORIES ROCK LEFT-WING PRIMARIES
A voting booth is seen. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

Smith recorded just over 50% of the vote by Wednesday morning, and was declared the winner by the Associated Press.
Smith told the Detroit News he is "humbled and honored that Republicans have chosen me to take the fight to Kristen McDonald Rivet."

She defeated the GOP's Paul Junge by about six points in 2024's contests.

title: Republicans move to oust embattled Florida GOP lawmaker in bitter primary fight
summary: Reps. Cory Mills, Chuck Edwards and Max Miller face misconduct allegations that now threaten GOP control of Congress heading into midterms. Edwards has dropped his campaign.
story: Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., is denying allegations from a source familiar to Fox News that the Justice Department is investigating him, claiming a Florida Republican primary opponent is behind it. (Credit: Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
House GOP divisions are erupting on the midterm campaign trail as Republicans fight an uphill battle to keep control of Congress for the latter half of President Donald Trump's term.

The infighting touched down in Florida on Wednesday, where two House Republicans are endorsing a primary opponent to incumbent Rep. Cory Mills, R-Fla., who is facing multiple investigations into his finances and allegations of domestic abuse, among other claims. Mills has denied any wrongdoing.

Reps. Mike Haridopolos, R-Fla., and Anna Paulina Luna, R-Fla., announced they're backing former local TV anchor Ryan Elijah for Mills' seat and said they "urge our fellow Republicans to join us in supporting him."

"Ryan Elijah is an excellent candidate and will ensure victory for us in Florida 7," Haridopolos told Fox News Digital. The Florida congressman will be in attendance at Mills' debate against Elijah on Wednesday night and plans to sit next to the candidate's wife.
GOP PARTY FISSURES EXPOSED IN BATTLE FOR S.C. SENATE SEAT TO REPLACE GRAHAM: 'I DON'T LIKE HEARING THAT'

Rep. Cory Mills (R-FL) talks to reporters at the U.S. Capitol on April 22, 2026 in Washington, DC. The House Ethics Committee is investigating Mills for allegations of sexual misconduct and campaign finance violations. Mills is denying any wrongdoing and said he will not step down.  (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Notably, President Donald Trump has endorsed Haridopolos, Luna and Mills for re-election — a fact Mills brought up in his response to Fox News Digital.

"I’m the only candidate in this race endorsed by President Donald Trump. Not once, not twice, but three times. I’m proud to have earned his trust because he knows I’ll continue fighting to advance the America First agenda and deliver results," Mills said. "The fact is, my office has returned more than $107 million to the people of Florida’s 7th District, led Florida in constituent services, built one of the strongest conservative voting records in Congress, and flipped this district from blue to red,and kept it red. My record speaks for itself."
It comes after another GOP source told Fox News Digital that some Florida Republicans were worried about the chances of keeping Mills' seat if he won the primary on Tuesday, Aug. 18.

The nonpartisan Cook Political Report downgraded its projection for Republicans from "Solid R" to "Likely R" earlier this year. And with a Cook rating of R+5, Democrats could be within striking distance if Republicans see a tough enough cycle in November.
Mills is under investigation by the House Ethics Committee and the Department of Justice (DOJ), according to a source, though he has consistently insisted that he has not done anything wrong.
WATCH: CORY MILLS BLASTS DOJ PROBE AS ‘POLITICAL OP' AHEAD OF FLORIDA PRIMARY

The Republican military veteran dismissed reports of a DOJ investigation as a "desperate lie" by his opponents and said on X late last month, "We are not aware of any DOJ investigation, nor has there been any confirmation of such investigation by DOJ or FBI, and would fully cooperate if there was one."
Fox News Digital reached out to Mills for a response to Haridopolos and Luna's endorsement.
Rep. Anna Paulina Luna speaks during the House Committee on Oversight and Accountability hearing on border and immigration issues in Washington, D.C., on Feb. 7, 2023. (Jack Gruber/USA TODAY)
Mills is one of several House Republicans whose allegations of misconduct are posing a headache for the GOP on the campaign trail.

Rep. Chuck Edwards, R-N.C., announced overnight that he would drop his re-election bid after an explosive report detailed sexual harassment accusations by two young female staffers. Edwards has denied those accusations but has admitted to at times making staff feel uncomfortable.
GOP LAWMAKER'S GIFTS, 'EFFUSIVE AFFECTION' TOWARD YOUNG STAFFERS DETAILED IN EXPLOSIVE ETHICS REPORT

And Rep. Max Miller, R-Ohio, has been accused of domestic abuse by his ex-wife and former father-in-law, Sen. Bernie Moreno, R-Ohio, and is facing pressure from congressional Republicans to drop out of his race as well. One House GOP source called the situation a "f---ing trainwreck" in comments to Fox News Digital.

Miller has denied any wrongdoing and asked the House Ethics Committee to initiate an investigation in order to clear his name. The former Trump aide has resisted calls to exit the race, insisting he will win in November and that the public accusations from his ex-wife are a bid to derail his political career.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
All three House seats are on the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) target list, meaning Democrats are pouring money and resources into those races.
One House Republican, who was granted anonymity to speak freely, told Fox News Digital that all three should drop out of their races, stating, "We must lead by example."

title: Political newcomer seeks to unseat twin of Trump impeachment foe in swing Virginia district
summary: Three GOP political newcomers battled it out in Virginia 7th Congressional District to challenge Rep. Eugene Vindman, twin brother of Trump impeachment witness Alexander Vindman.
story: Fox News correspondent Christina Coleman reports on Trump-endorsed candidates defeating incumbents in Indiana and Vivek Ramaswamy’s Ohio gubernatorial primary win on ‘Hannity.’
Douglas Ollivant decisively beat two fellow political newcomers in the Republican primary contest to take on incumbent Rep. Eugene Vindman, D-Va., in November.

Vindman, whose twin brother is a high-profile foe of President Donald Trump, currently represents Virginia's 7th Congressional district, a seat previously held by the state's Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger.

The Republican primary race between Ollivant, Rick Smithers and Philip Harding was unique in that none of the candidates had held elected office before, though two have government experience. The lack of reliable polling made it difficult to foretell who would emerge triumphant — but Ollivant ran away with victory, earning 56.6% of the vote compared to Harding's 30.7% and Smithers' 12.8%.
A voter casts their ballot at a polling location. (Graeme Sloan/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
THE BALLOT BOX SHOWDOWNS THIS MONTH THAT YOU NEED TO WATCH

Ollivant is a retired Army officer who served as the National Security Council director for Iraq during the George W. Bush administration. He worked as a national security analyst and consultant after that.
Smithers is a pastor and construction business owner who branded himself as the biggest outsider in the race.
Harding is a businessman with a bachelor's degree from Harvard University. He also earned his graduate degree from the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.
All three candidates have generally aligned themselves with Donald Trump, though the president did not endorse anyone in the race.
FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS: DEMOCRATS LEAD IN THE HOUSE, BUT REDISTRICTING KEEPS THE GOP IN THE GAME
According to FEC data, Ollivant had the cash advantage, raising $251,134. Harding raised $125,916 before primary Election Day, and there was no reported fundraising data for Smithers.
Rep. Eugene Vindman is speaking out against the U.S. move to halt some weapon shipments to Ukraine. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)

Virginia's 7th Congressional District, located in the northeastern part of the state and encompassing Culpeper and Fredericksburg east into Stafford, Spotsylvania, Caroline and parts of Prince William County, is considered a true swing state.
Vindman, who ran unopposed this time around, won the vacant seat by only three points.
SCOOP: HOUSE REPUBLICANS TARGET DOZENS OF VULNERABLE DEMOCRATS ON EVE OF TAX FILING DEADLINE

As Democrats hope to retain the seat in November, Republicans are eyeing it as a potential flip, which would be a welcome pickup as the GOP fights tooth-and-nail to keep control of Congress, a historically difficult feat for the party in power during a midterm election year.

Vindman's twin brother Alexander is a longtime foe of Trump. Alexander Vindman is a former military official, and the then-National Security Council director for European affairs testified against Trump during the first failed impeachment attempt in 2019.

National Security Council aide Lt. Col. Alexander Vindman testifies before the House Intelligence Committee on Capitol Hill in Washington, Nov. 19, 2019, during a public impeachment hearing of President Donald Trump's efforts to tie U.S. aid for Ukraine to investigations of his political opponents. (Andrew Harnik/AP Photo)

Alexander is an ardent defender of Ukraine, and became a central figure of the impeachment attempt, claiming that in a phone call with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, Trump attempted to make military aid for the embattled European nation contingent on an investigation into the Biden family's involvement in Ukrainian business activities.
