title: 10-year-old boy recounts near-drowning as family reveals friendship with California teen lifeguard hero
summary: Nathaniel Rai recalls the terrifying surf rescue that saved his life as his family opens up about the close friendship they formed with the California teen hero.
story: Nathaniel Rai, 10, shares new details in an interview with Fox News Digital about his terrifying drowning experience and the remarkable friendship his family formed with the teen lifeguard who rescued him.

The 10-year-old boy who nearly drowned after being swept into monster surf in Santa Cruz, California, late last month is sharing new details about the harrowing rescue that led to an unlikely friendship between his family and the teenage lifeguard who pulled him from the water.

Speaking to Fox News Digital, Nathaniel Rai said he lost consciousness and stopped breathing as 16-year-old California State Lifeguard Ryder Williams pulled him from the raging surf in a dramatic rescue captured on viral video. After being brought back to shore, Nathaniel began coughing up sand.

"Two more seconds in the water, he would be thrown another 15, 20 feet out," Nathaniel’s father, Sumit Rai, said. "And at that point, he'd be so far out, you can't see him, let alone rescue or retrieve him. And so he was in a near-death scenario."

Sumit said he is now Ryder's "biggest fan," adding that both families were contacted by the White House about honoring the teenager. He said he would fully support any recognition for Ryder, whom he now considers part of their "extended family."
TRUMP SAYS HEROIC TEEN LIFEGUARD WHO SAVED BOY FROM TOWERING WAVES DESERVES WHITE HOUSE HONOR
Sumit Rai stands alongside his son, Nathaniel Rai, at a Jiu-Jitsu tournament and a medical exhibit. (Provided to Fox News Digital)
According to the Rai family, the terrifying ordeal unfolded during what was supposed to be a relaxing beach vacation from Dallas with Nathaniel, his mother, Anna, and his 8-year-old sister.
Nathaniel said he was at the shallow end and had no intention of going deeper when a massive wave suddenly crashed over him.
"I started screaming for help," Nathaniel said. "I think I saw the lifeguard and then passed out."

Sumit said Ryder then swooped in with extreme determination, maintaining a firm grip on Nathaniel throughout the rescue, knowing that even a momentary loss of control could have sent the boy farther out into the dangerous surf.

"He was limp and unconscious in the water at that time when Ryder was holding him, which is really difficult to do, because he's carrying about 100 pounds of essentially dead weight through that current and those water forces," Sumit added.

Nathaniel Rai poses in a go-kart alongside California State Lifeguard Ryder Williams. Williams pulled Rai from dangerous rip currents during a dramatic ocean rescue in Santa Cruz, California, late July. (Provided to Fox News Digital/@castateparks/Instagram)

By the time Nathaniel was brought back to the beach, he had regained consciousness and was breathing again, but he was coughing up sand that had entered his lungs. Emergency personnel evaluated him and warned the family about "secondary drowning," potentially life-threatening complications that can develop hours after a drowning event.
Sumit said he was in Dallas when he learned what happened, but the viral video of the rescue added another layer of shock to the frightening ordeal.

"It was terrifying," he said. "When you look at that, you look at him submerged under the water, you look at the water conditions, the rip tides, the rip currents, the undertows, the 10-foot waves. I mean those are deadly water conditions."
CALIFORNIA LIFEGUARD SPEAKS OUT ON HEARTSTOPPING OCEAN RESCUE: 'I LOVE WHAT I DO'
During his free time, Nathaniel Rai plays chess and helps at his father's charity Cancer Check Labs. (Provided to Fox News Digital)

The father said he remains deeply grateful for Ryder's courage and determination, adding that he has become the teenager's biggest supporter, especially after President Donald Trump publicly suggested honoring him for his heroic efforts.

"I'm a fan of every single medal, award, honor, or recognition that he can get," Sumit said. "I'm 1 billion percent behind it. I am by far his biggest fan, and so I'd love to be there and advocate for him and support him."
After Nathaniel returned to Texas, the two families have reportedly developed a close bond, with Sumit saying Ryder and his family now feel like an extension of his own.
Sumit reportedly connected with Ryder's father, Shane, for a lengthy phone call, and the two have remained in daily contact.

Both parents have also discussed attending a UFC fight together after discovering their shared passion for UFC and MMA. Nathaniel has trained in MMA since he was 4 years old and is a Jiu-Jitsu champion at the U.S. Open Jiu-Jitsu World League.
"He liked UFC fights, like me and my dad and his dad," Nathaniel said.
"One of the things we're planning to do is all go to a fight together and meet up for that. So the four of us will go," his dad added.
According to Sumit, Ryder's father, Shane, is a retired firefighter, while Ryder hopes to follow in his father's footsteps and become one.
Coincidentally, Sumit runs Cancer Check Labs, a charity and business that screens firefighters for cancer risks associated with their profession.
Nathaniel has also been involved with the organization for several years, participating in lab work, exhibitions and even conferences, his father said.

"There were just multiple areas that we were connecting," Sumit said. "I think that's a bond that we're going to have for the rest of our lives. I think of them like an extended family at this point. Even I haven't even met them, which is kind of surreal. I'm looking forward to meeting them soon."

Nathaniel, who is preparing to enter sixth grade, said he is happy to be back in Dallas spending the rest of the summer with his father. In his downtime, he enjoys playing chess, watching movies and playing board games like Monopoly with his dad.

title: Marine veteran Las Vegas officer killed in shooting; armed suspect also dead
summary: A Las Vegas police officer and Marine veteran was fatally shot responding to a suspected gunman waving a firearm at a business on East Tropicana Avenue.
story: A Las Vegas police officer was killed while responding to a report of a suspected gunman, who was also killed in the exchange. (via Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department)
A Las Vegas police officer who was a Marine veteran was killed Tuesday while responding to a report of an armed person, authorities said. The suspect was also killed in the encounter.

Officers and police drones were sent to a business in the 4500 block of East Tropicana Avenue shortly before 4 p.m. after a caller reported that a person was waving a firearm and appeared to be intoxicated, according to the Las Vegas Metropolitan Police Department.

The suspect was pronounced dead at the scene.
A 30-year-old officer was wounded during the exchange and taken to University Medical Center, where he was pronounced dead, Clark County Sheriff Kevin McMahill said during a news briefing.

"A 30-year-old Las Vegas police officer was then worked on heroically by the Clark County Fire Department, other officers and EMS," McMahill said. "He was transported to UMC where nurses worked to save his life."

title: Lindsay Clancy's former nanny says she saw no warning signs despite postpartum disclosures
summary: Lindsay Clancy agreed to a stipulation in court as a state police trooper testified no usable fingerprints were found on a knife or exercise bands.
story: A former nanny testifies about her time in the Clancy household and Lindsay Clancy's postpartum struggles. The witness shares observations of the mother's daily routine, sleep difficulties, and medication changes.

A former nanny for Lindsay Clancy testified Wednesday that Clancy told her she was experiencing postpartum issues and having difficulty sleeping, but said she observed no change in Clancy’s demeanor and never believed the children were unsafe in her care.
"Not at all. She was a wonderful mom," Elaine Rossi said when a prosecutor asked whether she had any concerns about Clancy’s interactions with her children.
Rossi, who had worked as a nanny for about 15 years, said she cared for the Clancy children three days a week from September until early December 2022.
HEATED LINDSAY CLANCY COURTROOM EXCHANGE OVER 911 CALL, CRIME SCENE PHOTOS SETS STAGE FOR MOM’S MURDER TRIAL
Lindsay Clancy sits at the defense table during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., Wednesday, August 5, 2026. (David L. Ryan/Pool)

Clancy also told Rossi she was having difficulty sleeping and had been sleeping in the basement, the former nanny testified. On cross-examination, Rossi said she noticed Clancy appeared to be losing a significant amount of weight and had commented to her about it.

Rossi described Clancy as a loving and attentive mother who was concerned about the children’s safety and closely tracked Callan’s eating and sleeping schedule. She said Clancy left detailed instructions in a notebook but that she did not find the directions overbearing or controlling.
"She was a wonderful mom who loved her kids," Rossi testified. "She was very concerned with their safety."
Rossi said the family ended her employment after Thanksgiving because Clancy would not be returning to work and both parents planned to remain home with the children.

Elaine Rossi, the Clancy's nanny, testified that she and Clancy communicated via text messages and through a notebook left in the kitchen, agreeing with Assistant District Attorney Shanan Buckingham’s assessment that Clancy was "very particular" about Callan’s schedule.  (David L. Ryan/Pool)

Earlier Tuesday, Clancy spoke directly in court, repeatedly answering, "Yes, Your Honor," as she agreed to let prosecutors treat certain forensic facts as established. Hours later, a state police trooper testified that investigators recovered no usable fingerprints from a knife or three exercise bands.

The developments narrowed the Massachusetts mother’s murder trial toward its central dispute: whether Clancy was criminally responsible when her three children were killed inside the family’s Duxbury home.
Before jurors entered the courtroom, Judge William Sullivan questioned Clancy about a stipulation covering certain evidence.
WATCH: Lindsay Clancy questioned by judge before giving up key rights at murder trial

"You understand that by signing the stipulation, you’re agreeing that the Commonwealth does not have to prove these certain facts that are contained in the stipulation," Sullivan said. "Do you understand that?"
"Yes, Your Honor," Clancy replied.

Defendant Lindsay Clancy listens during her murder trial at Plymouth Superior Court in Plymouth, Mass., on Thursday, July 30, 2026. (CJ Gunther/The Boston Herald via AP, Pool)
Asked whether anyone had forced or threatened her to accept the agreement, Clancy said, "No, Your Honor."
Sullivan found that Clancy was competent and had entered the stipulation "knowingly, intelligently, voluntarily and willingly."
LINDSAY CLANCY’S EX-HUSBAND DETAILS PILL USE AS EXPERT SAYS EVIDENCE COULD SHAPE MURDER TRIAL
WATCH: State crime lab toxicologist details positive drug test results in court

Defense attorney Kevin Reddington said the agreement would prevent prosecutors from calling dozens of witnesses solely to establish the chain of custody for blood, bodily fluids, exercise bands and DNA evidence.
"We have not been contesting the government’s case in chief, if you will," Reddington said.

The stipulation is not a guilty plea or an admission that Clancy was criminally responsible for the deaths of Cora, 5, Dawson, 3, and Callan, 8 months.
WATCH: Former prosecutor explains strategy behind Lindsay Clancy evidence agreement

Margaret McLean, a former criminal prosecutor and trial attorney who teaches law at Boston College’s Carroll School of Management, said the agreement allows the defense to steer jurors away from repetitive forensic testimony and toward Clancy’s mental state.
LINDSAY CLANCY’S HUSBAND COULD TESTIFY FOR HER AT TRIAL OVER DEATHS OF THEIR THREE CHILDREN

"The legal strategy behind the move by the defense is to steer the jury’s focus away from the horrific nature of the acts and to that central issue of criminal intent, or what we would call mens rea," McLean told Fox News Digital.
McLean said Clancy’s measured responses Tuesday should not be taken as evidence of her mental condition on Jan. 24, 2023.

"She sounded rational. She understands what she’s doing," McLean said. "But remember, the Commonwealth’s burden of proof is to prove that she was sane beyond a reasonable doubt at the time the crimes were committed -- not today, not two weeks ago."

Later, Massachusetts State Police Trooper Jonathan O’Loughlin testified about examining a knife and three exercise bands collected from the home.

O’Loughlin said the knife contained an area of friction-ridge impression, but investigators could not use it to identify anyone.
"There was not enough characteristics or minutia to do any comparison," O’Loughlin said, adding that the impression had "no value."

Defendant Lindsay Clancy on Monday, Aug. 3, 2026, the fifth day of testimony at Plymouth Superior Court for her murder trial. Clancy is charged with three counts of murder in connection with the death of her three young children in 2023 at their Duxbury home. Clancy says she was suffering from postpartum psychosis and is not criminally responsible. (Greg Derr/Pool/The Patriot Ledger)
The yellow, black and blue exercise bands similarly produced no impressions suitable for comparison.

"The bottom line is that you didn’t get any fingerprints," Reddington said.
"Correct," O’Loughlin replied.

Lindsay Clancy's three children, 5-year-old Cora, 3-year-old Dawson and 8-month-old Callan. (Lindsay Marie Clancy facebook)

O’Loughlin said fingerprints are "very, very, very fragile" and can be affected by an object’s texture, environmental conditions, movement, grip strength or whether a surface was wiped.

McLean said the absence of identifiable prints could make jurors wonder whether gloves were used or the items were wiped, potentially viewing the missing prints as evidence of planning.

The defense, she said, can counter that jurors must not "speculate on something that’s not in evidence."

title: Mom of 4 recovering after suspected spider bite leads to severe complications: reports
summary: Britagne Miller reportedly spent weeks hospitalized, including time in intensive care, after a suspected spider bite was followed by surgery and infections.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Kansas mother of four is reportedly recovering after a suspected spider bite led to surgery, serious infections and a weeks-long hospital stay.

Britagne Miller of Goddard — about 14 miles west of Wichita — said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children at Cheney Lake May 28, when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her, according to local outlets KAKE and FOX Kansas.
Four days later, the area around one bite on her calf became swollen and painful, prompting her to seek medical care, FOX Kansas reported.
"This one kept swelling and swelling, and it was like, you know, a fire stir that's metal," Miller told KAKE. "It was like shooting down my leg into my foot, and it felt like it was being stabbed."
GIANT GOLDEN SPIDERS COULD SPREAD THIS SUMMER; EXPERTS DOWNPLAY HEALTH RISK
Britagne Miller said she was sitting around a campfire with her husband and children May 28 when several spiders crawled on her and apparently bit her. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)
Miller was admitted to Wesley Hospital in Wichita June 4 and underwent surgery, according to KAKE and a GoFundMe created by her husband, Jake Miller.
Her treatment was complicated by existing blood-clotting disorders, liver problems and allergies to certain medications, KAKE reported.
Miller later developed infections. Doctors also determined she was suffering from end-stage liver failure and warned her family that her condition could be fatal, according to KAKE.
Miller, who chose to continue treatment rather than enter hospice care, said she remembers little from her time in intensive care, according to the outlet.
BULL BISON SENDS YELLOWSTONE VISITOR FLIPPING THROUGH THE AIR IN CAMPGROUND ATTACK CAUGHT ON VIDEO
Britagne Miller said she remembers little from her time in intensive care. (Jake Miller via GoFundMe)
She was released from the hospital July 11 and is continuing her recovery at home.

Miller now requires home health care, physical therapy and regular visits with specialists. She also hopes to receive a liver transplant but is not yet eligible to be placed on the transplant list, according to KAKE and the GoFundMe.
Doctors have not confirmed what kind of spider bit her, KAKE reported.
Dr. Raymond Cloyd, a horticultural entomologist at Kansas State University, told KAKE the brown recluse and black widow are two venomous spiders commonly found in Kansas.
TEXAS TEEN BITTEN BY BARRACUDA IN POPULAR VACATION SPOT AFTER BRACELET GLINTS IN WATER

Cloyd advised sealing cracks and using caution with boxes, shoes and other undisturbed items, KAKE reported.

title: Man arrested at Trump golf course ahead of president’s visit allegedly had weapons cache
summary: A man allegedly photographing security preparations at Trump National Golf Club was found with weapons, body armor and concerning notebooks.
story: Fox News senior national correspondent Kevin Corke reports on the details surrounding the arrest of an armed suspect at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif., on 'Jesse Watters Primetime.'

A California man was arrested Sunday at Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes after allegedly monitoring security planning activities days before the president’s visit, and was later found with a cache of weapons and body armor, authorities said.
Jeanine John Taele, 38, of Downey, pleaded not guilty Tuesday to four criminal charges stemming from his arrest outside the golf course days before President Donald Trump's scheduled visit.
Trump arrived in Los Angeles late Tuesday for a Republican National Committee fundraiser.

A Los Angeles County judge set Taele's bail at $250,000, ordered him not to possess any weapons, barred him from Trump National Golf Club and prohibited him from leaving California while the case is pending.
His next court appearance is scheduled for Aug. 26, for a preliminary hearing setting and bail review.
TWO YEARS AFTER BUTLER, THREATS AGAINST TRUMP KEEP ASSASSINATION ATTEMPT IN SHARP FOCUS

According to the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, the investigation began Sunday, when plainclothes federal agents spotted Taele walking the grounds of Trump National Golf Club while taking photographs and videos and appearing to monitor security-planning activities.

Deputies from the Lomita Sheriff's Station responded around 3:30 p.m. and contacted Taele. During a pat-down, deputies allegedly recovered a 16-round magazine loaded with hollow-point ammunition from Taele's pants pocket.

Authorities then searched his vehicle, which was parked in the golf course parking lot, and recovered a loaded pistol with a round in the chamber, along with another loaded magazine containing hollow-point ammunition.
Jeanine John Taele, 38, pleaded not guilty to four criminal charges stemming from his arrest outside the golf course days before President Donald Trump's scheduled visit. (FBI)
Taele claimed he was employed by the State Department and was at the site for a security detail.

He was initially arrested on suspicion of carrying a concealed firearm and possessing prohibited ammunition. Prosecutors later charged him with receiving a large-capacity magazine, carrying a concealed firearm in a vehicle and possession of a short-barreled rifle or shotgun.
The discovery prompted detectives with the Sheriff's Department's Major Crimes Bureau assigned to the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force to obtain a search warrant for Taele's Downey home.
The entrance to Trump National Golf Club Los Angeles, in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif. (AP Photo/John Antczak, File)

Investigators said they recovered an illegally modified AR-platform rifle; a 1911 .45-caliber pistol; an AR-platform upper receiver; body armor; high-capacity magazines; bulk pistol and rifle ammunition; two radio signal devices; and multiple notebooks containing what authorities described as "concerning statements."

Separately, prosecutors also charged Taele with second-degree robbery in connection with an alleged Nov. 4, 2025, incident that was already under investigation by the El Segundo Police Department before Sunday's arrest at the golf course.

The investigation is being conducted jointly by the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department, the FBI's Joint Terrorism Task Force and the U.S. Secret Service. Officials said additional charges could be filed as the investigation continues.

"With respect to this defendant, we do not comment on the specifics of protective intelligence matters. However, the U.S. Secret Service thoroughly investigates any information or activity that may reasonably be perceived as a protective intelligence concern or indicate a potential threat or directed interest toward any individual under Secret Service protection," the U.S. Secret Service said in a statement.

"We are grateful to our partners at the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department and the Joint Terrorism Task Force for their continued support and strong partnership in advancing our shared investigative and protective missions," it added.
Authorities said they have identified no credible threat to the surrounding community but noted the investigation remains active.

The FBI's Los Angeles Field Office confirmed to Fox News Digital that the bureau's Joint Terrorism Task Force is continuing to investigate the case with the U.S. Secret Service and the Los Angeles County Sheriff's Department but declined to comment further because the investigation remains ongoing.
President Donald Trump and Trump National Golf Club in Rancho Palos Verdes, Calif.   (Fox News)

A spokesperson for The Trump Organization thanked the agencies involved in the response.

"We are incredibly grateful to the local law enforcement, the United States Secret Service, the FBI, and all supporting agencies for their swift response and dedication to keeping everyone safe," the spokesperson said.
Trump briefly addressed the incident on Tuesday, saying only consequential presidents are targeted.
"Well, the only thing I get a little solace from is, they say only consequential presidents. And I am definitely consequential," he said during an appearance on "Fox News @ Night."

title: More than half of some US weapons stockpiles used in Iran war, raising concerns about China threat
summary: CSIS warns depleted U.S. weapons stockpiles from the Iran war could embolden China as President Xi watches munitions levels amid Taiwan tensions.
story: ‘Special Report’ anchor Bret Baier has the details on the Iran conflict’s impact on the United States' missile defense stockpiles.

Some estimates show the U.S. has used more than half of its stockpiles of some weapons systems in the war with Iran. The Center for Strategic and International Studies found the U.S. has enough missiles to continue fighting in Iran under any plausible scenario, but the group says the true issue with the shrinking stockpiles is future wars.

"We can go on against Iran for quite a long time, even if we've used half the inventory. That means that half the inventories are still available," said Mark Cancian, a retired U.S. Marines colonel and senior advisor with the CSIS Defense and Security Department.
"The risk is about a future conflict in the Western Pacific against China."
Cancian pointed to reports that military officials have grown more concerned over the U.S. weapons inventory when factoring in other possible conflicts, such as one with China.
WEAPONS STOCKPILE SHORTAGES IMPACTING MILITARY STRATEGY IN THE MIDEAST

"The depletion of munitions was a major topic and a major reason for the suspension of air attacks," Cancian said. "Our inventories were getting way below what the war planners wanted. That might encourage China to do something."

Almost one-third of Tomahawk missiles have been used since the war in Iran began. Nearly two-thirds of Patriot missile interceptors have been depleted. Just over half of precision strike missiles remain.
President Donald Trump insists the U.S. has plenty of munitions to continue in Iran.
A rendered image of a Tomahawk missile (Provided to Fox News Digital)
"We have a lot of ammunition, different types," President Trump said in July. "I mean, more than we could ever use, no matter what. But we have a lot. I'd like to have more, to be honest."
HEGSETH DISMISSES ‘FOOLISH’ US STOCKPILE CONCERNS AS IRAN CONFLICT TESTS MUNITIONS
CSIS notes many munition stockpiles are substantial but focused its analysis on seven key weapons that have been effective in Iran and would also be valuable in a possible Pacific conflict.
An Iranian missile is launched during a military exercise in an undisclosed location in Iran Aug. 20, 2025.  (Iranian Army/WANA/Handout via Reuters)

"We have a defense industrial base that needs to be fixed at a very critical time in our history with the conflict in the Middle East," Rep. Michael McCaul, R-Texas, said. "President Xi of China is watching our stockpiles very closely as he contemplates threatening behavior towards the Taiwan straits, and, so, it all kind of factors in together here. And to be a strong United States, we need a strong military and project strength abroad."
The Pentagon is requesting significant increases in spending for weapons manufacturing, and lawmakers from both sides of the aisle believe the funding is of importance.
TRUMP IS PROVING THAT THE WAY TO BETTER OUR MILITARY IS TO SECURE OUR SUPPLY CHAINS

"Look, I have real concerns about our defense industrial base, and God forbid we find ourselves in a lengthy, serious war in our ability to produce what we need," Rep. Chris Deluzio, D-Pa., said. "I actually think it's a place where you can get some cooperation across the parties who want to see us re-industrialize."

The Pentagon’s budget request for fiscal year 2027 includes $5.8 Billion for Tomahawk missiles, an increase of 513% from the fiscal year 2026 request. Proposed spending for precision strike missiles is 245% higher, Terminal High Altitude Area Defense (THAADS) is up 650% and the request for Patriot Missile Segment Enhancement is 927% higher.

"Listen, if it's a $1.5 trillion package for defense, I'm all in. I really am," Rep. Troy Nehls, R-Texas, said. "The munitions are going to be there. We're going continue to do what we have to do to protect the world, protect Israel and everybody else in the region."
U.S. Central Command said it carried out another wave of airstrikes against Iran July 17, 2026. (CENTCOM)
If and when the funding is approved, it could take years for the new munitions to reach the battlefield.

"It takes quite a long time for the U.S. to produce new interceptors. They're complex manufacturing assemblages, and thus depleting those stockpiles does leave the U S materially worse off than it otherwise would have been in the current conflict," said UC Berkeley Senior Research Scholar Cameron Tracy.

The Patriot missiles requested in the fiscal year 2027 budget likely will not be available on the front line for another 3½ years. The Tomahawk estimated delivery time sits at almost four years. Some munitions orders could take as long as five years.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE U.S. NEWS

"Before the war, it would typically take about two years for the first system to arrive and then another year after that for the last," Cancian said. "You have to sign a contract, and then the manufacturer has to go out with the subcontractors and get all the materials. With the war, those timelines have been extended."

The Trump administration has created framework agreements with contractors to increase production capacity for key munitions. The deals call for new facilities, ambitious timelines and additional weapons systems.

"You can increase production capacity — we are doing that — [for] Patriot and many other systems. First, you have to recruit more people and train them up," Cancian said. "Then you can expand your facilities, but that takes time. You got to build the facilities, and you got to get all the permits and everything else. So, it can be done. We're seeing it happen, but, again, it takes time."

title: Florida 3-year-old dies after tragic incident involving common play toy at babysitter's house
summary: A 3-year-old girl was found unresponsive with her head trapped inside a toy kitchen at a babysitter's home in Boynton Beach, Florida, police said.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.
A Florida family is mourning its 3-year-old daughter after police said she became trapped in a toy kitchen play set while at a babysitter's home.
The girl, identified by loved ones as Briella, died July 27, four days after Boynton Beach police said she was found unresponsive with her head stuck inside the play set.
Officers rushed to the Meadows of Boynton Beach community shortly after 11 a.m. on July 23 after receiving a report of a child who was not breathing.
Police immediately began life-saving measures before Boynton Beach Fire Rescue transported the toddler to a nearby hospital, where she remained in critical condition until her death.
DAYCARE OPERATOR ARRESTED AFTER 3-YEAR-OLD WAS LEFT UNCONSCIOUS IN POOL FOR 20 MINUTES, DIED
Briella smiles in a family photo before the tragic incident that claimed the Florida toddler's life. (GoFundMe)
Investigators said the 3-year-old and her sibling were at a babysitter's home when the incident happened.
According to Boynton Beach police, the babysitter had left the residence and placed the children in the care of the babysitter's spouse.
While the children played downstairs, the spouse remained upstairs, periodically checking on them and bringing them snacks, police said.
TENNESSEE WOMAN ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY TRYING TO DROWN ONE OF HER CHILDREN IN BACKYARD POOL
Briella, the 3-year-old Florida girl who died following a tragic incident at a babysitter's home, is pictured with another child in an undated photo. (GoFundMe)
During one of those checks, the spouse found the toddler with her head stuck inside the toy kitchen, police said.
The spouse freed the child and immediately began performing life-saving measures until first responders arrived.
Police said the child's sibling told investigators that some of the children's toys had fallen inside the play kitchen. The toddler apparently became trapped while trying to retrieve them.
Authorities have not announced any criminal charges, and the investigation remains ongoing.
In a GoFundMe created following Briella's death, loved ones remembered the little girl as "a bright light in the lives of so many."
Loved ones remembered Briella as a bright light after the 3-year-old died following a tragic incident at a Florida babysitter's home. (GoFundMe)

"She had a kind heart, a beautiful spirit, and a smile that could light up any room," the fundraiser said. "She touched countless lives with her love, laughter, and compassion, and the impact she made will never be forgotten."

The fundraiser said donations will help the family cover funeral and memorial expenses as they navigate the devastating loss.
"She will forever be loved, forever missed, and forever in our hearts," the fundraiser said.

title: Kentucky child killer walks free as family says justice failed despite years of legal fights
summary: Ronald Exantus walked free after serving his sentence for the 2015 home invasion that killed 6-year-old Logan Tipton despite Logan's Law reforms.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

The Kentucky father whose 6-year-old son was stabbed to death while sleeping says the man found not guilty by reason of insanity in the killing received "a slap on the wrist" after being released from prison July 29 upon completing his sentence for assaulting three surviving family members.

Ronald Exantus was released from Kentucky Department of Corrections custody July 29 after completing the sentence imposed for assaulting Logan Tipton's father and sisters during the 2015 home invasion that left the 6-year-old dead.

The case stunned Kentucky after prosecutors said Exantus broke into the Tipton family's home on Dec. 7, 2015, and fatally stabbed 6-year-old Logan Tipton while he slept. Logan's father and two sisters were also stabbed but survived the attack. A jury later found Exantus not guilty by reason of insanity on murder and burglary charges but guilty but mentally ill on assault charges involving the surviving family members.
The assault convictions resulted in the prison sentence he completed last week, reigniting outrage from the Tipton family and renewed questions about Kentucky's criminal justice system.
FLORIDA AG SEEKS JUDGE'S IMPEACHMENT AFTER BABY DROWNING COVID INSANITY ACQUITTAL
Ronald Exantus served 11 years, nine months and 18 days before he was released July 29.  (Fox News Channel)

"The judge and jury gave this monster a slap on the wrist while handing down a life sentence to my family," Logan's father, Dean Tipton, wrote on Facebook after Exantus' release. "Make sure to lock your doors and keep an eye out for baby killers. He will be released today. Watch your house, your neighbors house, your kids, your neighbors kids. He could be coming to your town. Kentucky justice at its finest."
According to the Kentucky Department of Corrections, Exantus completed the sentence imposed by the court after receiving sentence credits required under Kentucky law.
HOUSE DEMOCRAT BLASTED AFTER EARLY RELEASE LAW FREED INMATES LATER CHARGED WITH MURDER
A booking photo of Ronald Exantus, who was found not guilty by reason of insanity in the killing of 6-year-old Logan Tipton and later convicted of assault charges. (Kentucy Online Offender Lookup)

"Ronald Exantus has served the sentence issued by the Woodford Circuit Court and has been released," the department told Fox News Digital. "He is no longer in the custody of the Department of Corrections."

Corrections officials emphasized that juries and courts determine an offender's sentence, while the department is responsible for calculating that sentence under Kentucky law, including applying any earned statutory sentence credits.
Once Exantus reached his legally calculated sentence expiration date, the agency said it no longer had authority to keep him incarcerated.
The department also stressed that the Kentucky Parole Board "did not release Exantus, and he was not released early."

Exantus was briefly released on mandatory reentry supervision in October 2025 before moving to Florida, where authorities said he violated the conditions of his supervision by failing to register as a convicted felon.

He was returned to Kentucky after the violation, and the Parole Board revoked his mandatory reentry supervision, ordering him back to prison. The department said he ultimately remained incarcerated until completing his sentence July 29.
NEWSOM-BACKED LAW LETS ILLEGAL IMMIGRANT CHILD RAPIST SEEK EARLY RELEASE AGAIN AS DA URGES 'STOP THE MADNESS'
Prosecutors said Ronald Exantus received nearly nine years of sentence credit, as is required under Kentucky law, that accelerated his release. (Woodford County Detention Center)
Kentucky Attorney General Russell Coleman said his office worked alongside prosecutors, law enforcement and corrections officials to keep Exantus incarcerated for as long as the law allowed.

In a November 2025 letter to the Kentucky Parole Board, Coleman urged board members to revoke Exantus' mandatory reentry supervision after Exantus violated its conditions in Florida and required him to serve the remainder of his sentence in prison.
"The public good and common sense demand nothing less," Coleman wrote, calling Logan Tipton's killing "every parent's worst nightmare."
The Parole Board ultimately revoked Exantus' mandatory reentry supervision and ordered him back to prison after finding he violated the terms of his supervision.

Ahead of Exantus' scheduled release, the Kentucky Justice and Public Safety Cabinet also notified the trial judge, Commonwealth's Attorney Kelli Kearney and defense counsel that they could pursue involuntary hospitalization proceedings before his sentence expired if they believed it was appropriate under Kentucky law.
The Department of Corrections said it lacked the legal authority to continue holding Exantus once he completed his sentence unless another lawful basis for detention was established.
In a November 2025 interview with WKYT, Coleman said "the system failed the Tipton family," while pledging to pursue every legal avenue available to keep Exantus incarcerated.
CALIFORNIA MOM RIPS NEWSOM-BACKED 'DIVERSION PROGRAM' THAT APPEARS TO BENEFIT HER SON'S KILLER
Undated photo of Logan Tipton (GoFundMe)
Public outrage over Logan’s case helped spur Kentucky lawmakers to pass House Bill 422, known as Logan’s Law, which Gov. Andy Beshear signed in April.

The law revised Kentucky’s insanity defense and mandatory reentry supervision rules in response to issues raised by Exantus’ case. But because it does not apply retroactively, it had no effect on Exantus' sentence or July 29 release.
State Rep. Daniel Fister, who helped champion the legislation, called Exantus' release "heartbreaking" and vowed to continue working with the Tipton family to strengthen Kentucky's criminal laws.
"My heart breaks yet again for the Tipton family and our community as we are once again forced to endure the pain and uncertainty caused by Ronald Exantus," Fister told Fox News Digital.
NORTH CAROLINA TEACHER'S KILLING REIGNITES SCRUTINY OF ROY COOPER'S CRIMINAL JUSTICE RECORD IN SENATE RACE
Dean Tipton stands alongside Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear and others after signing House Bill 422, known as Logan's Law. (Dean Tipton Facebook)
"No family should have to endure this kind of trauma, and every Kentuckian deserves confidence that our justice system will protect innocent victims and hold violent offenders accountable."
Fister said Logan's Law was "an important step forward" but promised lawmakers would continue pursuing reforms to better protect Kentucky families.
"We owe it to Logan's memory and to every family across the Commonwealth to continue pursuing reforms that put the safety of innocent Kentuckians first," he said.

Fister also said Exantus' release underscores broader concerns about Kentucky's criminal justice system, arguing that delays in implementing provisions of House Bill 5 have allowed some violent offenders to become eligible for parole earlier than lawmakers intended.
DEVASTATED MOTHER BLAMES SOFT-ON-CRIME POLICIES AFTER CAREER CRIMINAL IS CHARGED IN SON’S DEATH
"That is deeply troubling for victims and their families who deserve confidence that violent criminals will be held fully accountable," he said.
State Rep. T.J. Roberts, who also helped author Logan's Law, called Exantus' release "a gross miscarriage of justice."

"Once again, Kentucky's judiciary has failed the Tipton family," Roberts told Fox News Digital. "The monster who killed Logan Tipton should spend the rest of his life in prison, at a minimum, and his release is a gross miscarriage of justice. The Tipton family, all of Kentucky, and all of America deserve so much better than what this government offers to the innocent."
Roberts noted that the U.S. Constitution prohibits lawmakers from retroactively increasing criminal penalties, meaning Logan's Law could not be applied to Exantus after his conviction.
GIANNO CALDWELL: FOUR YEARS AFTER MY BROTHER’S MURDER, I’M MARCHING FOR JUSTICE
Logan Tipton in his football uniform (Dean Tipton Facebook)

Calling Logan's Law "a great first step," Roberts said he plans to introduce additional legislation that would expand the availability of life without parole for murder convictions, strengthen victim notification requirements and further protect Kentuckians from violent offenders.
"I intend to file legislation to ensure our justice system protects the innocent, not violent offenders," he said.
Roberts also offered a message directly to the Tipton family.
"I want the Tipton family to know they have my support and the support of millions of people who have heard their story," he said. "God is with them, and we will not let Logan's life be forgotten."
BODYCAM FOOTAGE FUELS BACKLASH AFTER POLICE HANDCUFF DYING STABBING VICTIM
For Tipton, Exantus' release reopened wounds that have never healed.
"Knowing that this monster gets to walk free and live his life, while I lay in this bed and my baby boy is in the grave," he wrote. "This may be my breaking point."
Although Logan's Law has now taken effect, Tipton said he believes Kentucky must go further.
"So I've come to terms that even though we got Logans Law passed it is still not enough," he wrote. "Violent criminals should not be able to knock so much time off their sentence.
"Our judicial system as a whole needs to be over hauled and I am gonna fight for more change."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Despite helping inspire Logan's Law, the Tipton family says its fight is far from over. The family has launched a GoFundMe to help pay for attorneys as they pursue additional legal remedies and continue pushing for further criminal justice reforms.

"We turned our deepest grief into a fierce, relentless battle to change the law so no other family would ever have to suffer the way we have," the family wrote on the fundraising page. But while Logan's Law was signed this year, they noted it "does not retroactively stop our son's killer from being released."
"The fight is not over and we need your help," the family added.
Stepheny Price is a Writer at Fox News with a focus on West Coast and Midwest news, missing persons, national and international crime stories, homicide cases, and border security.

title: Air Force says two advanced stealthy aircraft are ahead of schedule, with first delivery set for 2027
summary: The B-21 Raider stealth bomber program accelerated 25% after a $4.5 billion funding boost, with Northrop Grumman targeting seven bombers annually.
story: Bill Hemmer and John Spencer, executive director of the Urban Warfare Institute, discuss the Pentagon's new initiative to oversee military drones and autonomous systems. Spencer emphasizes the necessity for the U.S. to lead in drone technology, citing lessons from the Ukraine war and the significant budget requested for research and development.

The Air Force says its next-generation B-21 Raider stealth bomber program is ahead of schedule, with the first operational aircraft expected to arrive at Ellsworth Air Force Base in South Dakota in 2027.

The service's sixth-generation F-47 fighter is also progressing faster than expected, according to Gen. Dale White, director of Critical Major Weapon Systems, who discussed both programs during the Air Force's Life Cycle Industry Days conference in Dayton, Ohio.
White said the B-21 acquisition program has accelerated by roughly 25% since a one-time $4.5 billion funding boost was included in the 2025 reconciliation bill.
The comments provide one of the clearest public updates yet on the status of the Air Force's two flagship next-generation aircraft programs.
AMERICA’S NEW STEALTH B-21 RAIDER TAKES NEXT STEP WITH SECOND BOMBER’S FIRST FLIGHT
A B-21 takes flight near Edwards Air Force base in September 2025. (Air Force)

The update comes months after the Air Force announced a second B-21 Raider joined flight testing at Edwards Air Force Base in California, a milestone officials at the time said would accelerate testing and weapons integration for America's first new long-range bomber in more than three decades.

White said the first operational B-21 is expected to be "on the ramp" at Ellsworth in 2027, with Northrop Grumman planning to eventually produce seven operational bombers annually. The Pentagon has requested $6.1 billion for the B-21 program in its fiscal year 2027 budget proposal.

Built by Northrop Grumman, the B-21 is designed to carry both conventional and nuclear weapons while penetrating advanced enemy air defenses. The aircraft is expected to eventually replace the B-1 Lancer and B-2 Spirit while operating alongside modernized B-52 Stratofortress bombers expected to remain in service into the middle of the century. The Air Force plans to acquire at least 100 B-21 bombers.
White also said planning for the Boeing-built F-47 has reached an "unprecedented maturity."
INSIDE AMERICA’S 6TH-GEN ARSENAL: B-21, F-47, AND THE FUTURE OF AIR DOMINANCE
The crew at a test flight of a B-21. (Air Force)

The Air Force plans to acquire 185 F-47 fighters, with the first flight scheduled for 2028. The aircraft will replace the F-22 Raptor as the service's primary air superiority fighter and is expected to operate alongside Collaborative Combat Aircraft, autonomous "loyal wingman" drones designed to support crewed aircraft in combat. The Pentagon has requested $5.03 billion for the F-47 program in its fiscal year 2027 budget request.
The B-21 Raider goes through testing at Edwards Air Force Base in California.  (Defense Visual Information Distribution Service)

title: Washington wildfire arson suspect previously charged with first-degree murder, records show
summary: Aaron Farinacci, charged with first-degree arson in Spokane's Old Trails Fire, previously pleaded guilty to manslaughter in a 2010 Arizona homicide.
story: Fox News’ Sarah Alegre reports on wildfires across Spokane County, Washington, destroying hundreds of structures and forcing thousands of residents to evacuate on ‘Special Report.’

The man accused of setting the largest of the wildfires that have destroyed hundreds of buildings and forced tens of thousands of people from their homes in eastern Washington was previously charged with first-degree murder before pleading guilty to a reduced manslaughter charge, court records show.

Aaron F. Farinacci, 37, was arrested Monday on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire, the largest of three blazes burning in and around Spokane, Washington's second-largest city.

The fires have destroyed at least 700 buildings and forced about 67,000 people to evacuate. Authorities have not alleged any connection between Farinacci and the other two fires, which remain under investigation.
WASHINGTON MAN ARRESTED ON ARSON CHARGE TIED TO DEVASTATING SPOKANE WILDFIRE
The arrest came hours after former Washington Gov. Jay Inslee, a Democrat, pointed to climate change as firefighters battled the region's destructive wildfires.
Aaron F. Farinacci was arrested on suspicion of first-degree arson in connection with the Old Trails Fire in eastern Washington. (Arizona Department of Corrections)
"Climate change isn't some existential global thing," Inslee said Monday. "It's our neighbors. It's our friends."

Court records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Farinacci was initially charged with first-degree murder and aggravated assault in a 2010 Arizona homicide before pleading guilty in 2012 to reduced charges of manslaughter and aggravated assault.
The Associated Press reported that Farinacci, then 21, fatally shot his father during an argument over washing dishes in Mesa, Arizona, in 2010. Farinacci also shot himself but survived.

A Maricopa County judge sentenced Farinacci to 12 years in prison after he pleaded guilty to manslaughter and aggravated assault. Arizona Department of Corrections records show he was released on Dec. 23, 2020.
FOLLOW THE FOX TRUE CRIME TEAM ON X
Aaron Farinacci, 37, was charged with first-degree arson. (Spokane County Sheriff’s Office)
Less than six years after his release from prison, Farinacci again found himself accused of a major crime.

The Spokane County Sheriff's Office said Major Crimes detectives and Washington State Department of Natural Resources fire investigators identified Farinacci as the suspect after developing probable cause during the investigation.

Detectives obtained arrest and search warrants before taking Farinacci into custody without incident at his Spokane residence, where he was booked into the Spokane County Jail on suspicion of first-degree arson.

Court records show witnesses first spotted Farinacci standing near the tree line where investigators later determined the fire started. When they returned about 10 minutes later, they saw him bent over facing the fence and vegetation. As their vehicle approached, Farinacci stood up and appeared "nervous," according to the affidavit.
SIGN UP TO GET THE LATEST TRUE CRIME NEWS
Firefighters respond to a wildfire near Spokane, Washington, on Aug. 2, 2026. (South Pend Oreille Fire Rescue / FOX Weather)

After returning home and noticing smoke rising from the same area, the witnesses flagged down an Airway Heights police officer and provided investigators with a physical description of the man and the clothing he was wearing.

Deputies initially detained and questioned Farinacci before releasing him as first responders focused on evacuating residents threatened by the rapidly growing fire, Nowels said. The affidavit states deputies had not yet determined the fire's origin or learned witnesses had seen Farinacci near the point investigators later identified as where the blaze began.
LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE
When deputies told Farinacci witnesses had seen him near the fire, he replied, "Those witnesses don't know the whole thing," the affidavit states.
As detectives reviewed witness statements, body camera footage and evidence gathered by fire investigators, they developed probable cause to arrest Farinacci.

Deputies said they found Farinacci carrying a butane lighter and a box of Gofire brand rain-ready, heavy-duty waterproof matches. The affidavit says the box originally contained 25 matches, with 14 remaining. Farinacci told deputies he bought the matches several days earlier and used them to light cigarettes if his lighter stopped working.
Fire investigators ruled out trains and nearby electrical infrastructure before concluding the blaze was consistent with an open flame from a lighter or match, the affidavit states.
GET BREAKING NEWS BY EMAIL
Chimneys are the only structures remaining in a residential neighborhood after a wildfire hit the northern part of Spokane, Washington, Monday, Aug. 3, 2026. (AP Photo / Lindsey Wasson)

Nowels said the first-degree arson charge reflected the evidence investigators currently have but cautioned that additional charges could be considered as the investigation continues and authorities assess the full scope of the fire's destruction.
The sheriff credited observant residents with helping investigators quickly identify the suspect.

"As it happens in so many critical cases, it was citizens who were paying attention to their surroundings, being aware and willing to step up and say something that led to the relatively quick apprehension of Mr. Farinacci," Nowels said.
Ana Dillon told Fox News Digital strangers are rarely seen on the family's dead-end road, making the man her father spotted near the tracks immediately stand out.
SEND US A TIP
Allen Sather stands in front of his 1968 Chevrolet C20 at the duplex he rented on W. Indian Trail Rd. that burned in a wildfire in Spokane, Washington, Sunday, Aug. 2, 2026. (AP Photo / Young Kwak)

"There's only two houses on this street," Dillon said. "If anyone is on this street, we most always call Crime Check. No one should be on this road. It's a closed road. Anyone standing and kneeling down by the train tracks that's not a city worker is a red flag."
GOT A TIP?
Moments after her father returned home, Dillon said she looked outside and saw "a huge cloud of white smoke, then black smoke" before calling 911.

"The fire was coming toward us, so we packed up everything, everyone and animals," Dillon said. "As we were leaving, they had caught that guy. My dad and son had to do a drive-by ID. Then we found out the next morning they let him go."
Farinacci made his first court appearance Tuesday afternoon, where a judge set bond at $1 million and adopted prosecutors' requested release conditions.

If released, Farinacci would be prohibited from possessing lighters, matches, torches or other fire-starting devices, have no contact with witnesses identified in the probable cause affidavit and remain within Spokane County unless otherwise authorized.

title: New York police official accused of driving getaway car for son in gang-related shooting
summary: Jennifer Lackard, a Mount Vernon deputy police commissioner, allegedly sped off with her son Chase after he shot at rival gang members near Bronx court.
story: Chase Lackard, son of Mount Vernon Deputy Police Commissioner Jennifer Lackard was shot on this Bronx bus in 2023. Lackard was fired after being accused of helping her son flee an alleged gang-related shooting in June 2026. (Peter Gerber)
A New York police official is being accused of serving as the getaway driver for her son in an apparent gang shooting in New York City, the New York Post reported Tuesday.

Police sources told the Post that Jennifer Lackard, a deputy police commissioner with the Mount Vernon Police Department, was arrested along with her son, Chase Lackard, 20, at their home Tuesday morning. Authorities said Chase was charged with shooting at rival gang members near the Bronx Criminal Court in late June.
Sources told the Post that Chase ran to his mother in her car after the shooting, and she sped off.
No one was injured in the shooting.
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMANDS RELEASED BY PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT IN BID TO IDENTIFY SENDER
Jennifer Lackard served as a deputy police commissioner with the Mount Vernon Police Department. (Theodore Parisienne / New York Daily News via Getty Images; Mt. Vernon Police Department)
Both the mother and son have been charged with attempted murder, attempted assault, criminal possession of a firearm, conspiracy and reckless endangerment.
The Mount Vernon Police Department said Tuesday that Lackard had been terminated effectively immediately.

"The allegations are unrelated to her duties with the Mount Vernon Police Department and do not stem from any conduct associated with the Department or the performance of her official responsibilities," the department wrote on social media.
ROMANIAN NATIONAL LEARNS FATE FOR SWATTING US OFFICIALS, INCLUDING MEMBERS OF CONGRESS, JUDGES

NYPD officers and detectives investigate after Chase Lackard, 19, was shot and wounded by police on White Plains Road near Lafayette Ave. in the Bronx on Nov. 22, 2024, in New York City. (Barry Williams / New York Daily News via Getty Images)
The incident was far from Chase's first run-in with law enforcement. He was shot by police in 2024 after allegedly wielding a gun during an argument.
He was also shot once before in 2023 by three other youths during a dispute on a bus. Chase is allegedly a member of the "Slutty Gang," according to the Post.

title: Russia deploys North Korean missile unit to Ukraine; Moscow-Pyongyang axis deepens: report
summary: A Ukrainian intelligence official says Russia is deploying a North Korean unit with up to 120 ballistic missiles in its war against Ukraine.
story: Fox News senior foreign affairs correspondent Greg Palkot discusses the Russian missile attack on the Ukranian capital Kyiv. At least 17 people were killed as tension between the two countries continues.

Russia has begun deploying a North Korean missile unit equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for use in its war against Ukraine, a Ukrainian intelligence official told told Reuters on Wednesday.

The reported escalation marks a deepening military partnership between Moscow and Pyongyang, with around 90 North Korean personnel expected to be stationed in Russia's western Voronezh region to support the new unit, according to Andrii Cherniak of Ukraine's Main Directorate of Intelligence (HUR).
Cherniak also claimed Pyongyang has already delivered a fresh batch of 40 KN-23 and KN-24 ballistic missiles to Russian forces, Reuters said.
RUSSIA LAUNCHES BALLISTIC MISSILE ATTACK ON KYIV HOURS AFTER ZELENSKYY WARNS OF MAJOR STRIKE

Russia has reportedly begun deploying a North Korean missile unit equipped with up to 120 ballistic missiles and six launchers for use in its war against Ukraine. (Alexander Kazakov/Pool/AFP via Getty Images)
Final details of the deployment are expected to be finalized during high-level bilateral talks next month.

The intelligence report follows a massive Russian barrage against Kyiv and the surrounding region on Aug. 4. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Moscow launched 24 ballistic missiles, four cruise missiles and 115 drones overnight, killing at least 17 people.
Zelenskyy argued more lives could have been saved had Western allies replenished Ukraine's depleted stockpiles of air defense interceptors.
Zelenskyy previously warned that Moscow had been preparing since June to receive additional North Korean military personnel in the Voronezh region, according to to reports.
RUSSIA UNLEASHES NEARLY 600 MISSILES AND DRONES ON KYIV IN DEADLIEST STRIKE SINCE MAY
Russian President Vladimir Putin has deepened his defensive ties with North Korea's Kim Jong Un. (Getty Images)
Cherniak told Reuters a Russian strike in late July marked the first recorded use of North Korean ballistic missiles against Ukrainian targets since August 2025.
According to HUR estimates, Russia has received approximately 150 KN-23 and KN-24 missiles from North Korea since late 2023.
Military analysts say Russia is increasingly relying on ballistic weapons because they require advanced defense systems — such as the U.S.-made Patriot — to intercept.

The Washington-based Institute for the Study of War (ISW) assessed that Russia is deliberately incorporating more ballistic missiles into its long-range strike packages to maximize pressure on Ukraine's limited air defenses.
ISW added that North Korea is gaining critical battlefield data from the conflict, allowing Pyongyang to refine its missile performance using Russian operational experience.
ALARMING MISSILE REPORT DRAWS FORCEFUL RESPONSE FROM TRUMP AS IRAN WAR TESTS AMERICA’S ARSENAL
North Korea has emerged as one of Moscow's key military allies. (KCNA via Reuters)
North Korea has emerged as one of Moscow's key military allies since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine began.
Reuters reported that Pyongyang has supplied millions of artillery shells and previously sent 14,000 troops to Russia's Kursk region to counter Ukraine's 2024 cross-border incursion.
Cherniak also noted that roughly 9,500 North Korean troops are still in Kursk, though they are not engaged in active combat right now.

A report by the Foundation for Defense of Democracies (FDD) states that, since Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine, North Korea has supplied Moscow with large quantities of artillery and rocket ammunition, cannon and rocket artillery systems and ballistic missiles.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The policy institute described the Russia-North Korea relationship as one of the "most consequential among the Axis" and the only partnership in which one member has deployed troops in combat to assist another.

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Nuclear experts urge Trump not to let Iran steer talks away from regime's atomic threat
summary: Nuclear experts urged President Trump to keep Iran’s nuclear program at the center of talks, warning Tehran could seek sanctions relief before addressing remaining nuclear capabilities.
story: The FDD's Andrea Stricker says Tehran is seeking control of the strategic waterway and sanctions relief before addressing its enriched uranium and nuclear infrastructure.

Iran’s top Revolutionary Guard commander declared Wednesday that Tehran would continue working on nuclear weapons as long as the United States and Israel possess them, intensifying concerns that Iran is using negotiations over the Strait of Hormuz to postpone concessions on its nuclear program.

"As long as the United States and Israel possess nuclear weapons, we will continue working on them for our national security," IRGC commander-in-chief Ahmad Vahidi said, according to a translation of remarks circulating Wednesday. "If they disarm, we will disarm."
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu responded by vowing that Israel would continue preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, with or without a diplomatic agreement.
WHO IS AHMAD VAHIDI? IRAN’S NEW IRGC CHIEF TIED TO GLOBAL ATTACKS AND ‘DEATH TO AMERICA’ IDEOLOGY
A map shows damage to Iran's Fordow nuclear site after being struck by the United States in Operation Midnight Hammer on June 22, 2025. (Fox News)

"Today, we heard the commander of the Revolutionary Guards, Vahidi, explicitly declare Iran’s intention to continue developing nuclear weapons — ‘continue,’ as he put it," Netanyahu said at a ceremony marking the reinterment of Shimon and Rivka Herzl, the grandparents of the founder of modern day Zionism, Theodor Herzl.
"Well, as prime minister of Israel, I too am determined to continue — to continue preventing Iran from possessing nuclear weapons," he said.
Netanyahu praised President Donald Trump as Israel’s greatest friend in the White House and expressed appreciation for the two countries’ joint efforts against Iran’s nuclear ambitions.

"Israel’s existence is not subject to negotiation," Netanyahu said. "With an agreement or without an agreement, I am determined — we are all determined — to do whatever is necessary to ensure our security and our future."
NETANYAHU'S ISRAEL GRAPPLES WITH TRUMP-IRAN DEAL AS DETAILS REMAIN UNCLEAR
President Pezeshkian said Iran would rebuild the nuclear facilities targeted by the U.S. and make them stronger in 2025. (Iranian Presidency/Handout/Anadolu via Getty Images)

The exchange came as nuclear experts urged Trump to keep Iran’s nuclear program at the center of negotiations, warning that Tehran could use the Hormuz crisis to secure sanctions relief and other concessions before addressing its remaining nuclear capabilities.
Trump told "Fox News at Night" Tuesday that military force remained an option if Iran abandoned the talks, while insisting Tehran could not be allowed to obtain a nuclear weapon.

"If they back out again, they’re going to get hit really hard," Trump told Fox News’ Trace Gallagher. "They know that. They understand that. I have no choice. They can’t have a nuclear weapon. It’s very simple.
"The hard hit is yet to come, and hopefully we won’t have to use it."

Trump said negotiators held an "all-day negotiation" Tuesday and described the discussions as "very good." He has said the talks would initially focus on reopening the Strait of Hormuz before turning to Tehran’s nuclear program.
TRUMP WARNS IRAN WILL BE HIT 'REALLY HARD' IF NUCLEAR NEGOTIATIONS COLLAPSE AGAIN
A satellite view of the Natanz nuclear facility and Pickaxe Mountain, near Natanz, Iran, June 30, 2026 (Vantor/Handout via Reuters)
Andrea Stricker, deputy director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies’ Nonproliferation and Biodefense Program, said that sequence could play directly into Iran’s strategy.

"It is in the Iranians’ interest to steer the negotiations toward the issues that they most care about," Stricker told Fox News Digital, including securing major U.S. concessions over Hormuz and "maintaining control of that crucial waterway that has proven a lifeline for Tehran to survive this war."
She said Iran would also seek oil sanctions relief and potentially relief from all U.S. sanctions, before addressing the nuclear file.

"If Tehran is able to structure the talks that way — and I’m concerned that Trump appears to be going along with that approach — there may be little left in terms of leverage to get big concessions from the Iranians on the nuclear file down the line," Stricker said.

There is evidence that Tehran has sought to sequence the talks in its favor. Axios reported in April that Iran proposed reopening the Strait of Hormuz and ending the war before beginning nuclear negotiations, potentially reducing U.S. leverage over enrichment and Iran’s enriched-uranium stockpile.

President Donald Trump, right, speaks alongside Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu with a model of Air Force One on the table during a meeting in the Oval Office of the White House April 7, 2025, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
The Washington Post later reported that Tehran was focused on preserving its leverage over Hormuz rather than engaging deeply on major nuclear restrictions.

Kelsey Davenport, director for nonproliferation policy at the Arms Control Association, agreed Iran is seeking to capitalize on the leverage it gained by disrupting maritime traffic through the Strait of Hormuz.

"The current focus on the Straits of Hormuz is not surprising. Iran is looking to capitalize on leverage gained by disrupting maritime traffic through the waterway and test if Trump is willing to negotiate in good faith," Davenport told Fox News Digital.
TRUMP WARNS IRAN FIGHTING ISN'T OVER AS HE VOWS US WILL 'WIN' AS TALKS FADE
Satellite imagery taken Jan. 30, 2026, shows a new roof over a previously destroyed building at Natanz nuclear site. (2026 Planet Labs PBC/Handout via Reuters)

She said Tehran understands that any durable agreement will ultimately have to address its nuclear program but said, "At the end of this conflict, Iran will still possess the capabilities necessary to build a bomb," Davenport said, "The relevant knowledge and nuclear expertise cannot be bombed away.

"Tehran retains key materials and technologies necessary to build a bomb," she added. "If left unchecked, the nuclear program will be a source of instability and renewed conflict, even if Iran does not resume more proliferation-sensitive nuclear activities."

A proposed agreement between Iran and Oman could give Tehran some control over ships entering the Persian Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz, a senior Iranian source and two regional officials told Reuters Wednesday. One regional source described the arrangement as a concession that had already been made, although the precise meaning of Iranian "control" remained under negotiation.
Iran is also seeking fees from ships traveling through the waterway, according to Reuters, while Washington has opposed both Iranian control and mandatory transit charges.
Stricker said postponing the nuclear issues would allow the regime to preserve its remaining enriched-uranium stockpiles and avoid fully dismantling its nuclear infrastructure.
She said Iran also wants to avoid accounting for its past nuclear weapons-related work or committing to end uranium enrichment and plutonium reprocessing.
The Bushehr nuclear plant in Iran April 29, 2024 (Morteza Nikoubazl/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
"Leaving them as a last-order issue in the negotiations likely means that we will not see the Iranians make big concessions and make a solid nuclear deal," Stricker said.
Davenport said the administration should prioritize restoring access for inspectors from the International Atomic Energy Agency before beginning detailed nuclear negotiations.

"The IAEA has not visited key Iranian nuclear sites in more than a year," she said. "It remains unclear how much of Iran’s nuclear infrastructure remains and where any gaps might be in trying to account for Iran’s nuclear materials."

She said renewed inspections would give Washington a clearer picture of Iran’s remaining facilities and materials, while helping negotiators design a verification regime capable of addressing any gaps.
Davenport also recommended pairing sanctions relief with specific, verifiable Iranian steps rather than negotiating one sweeping package.
"A series of smaller deals could build confidence in the process," she said.
Stricker urged the administration to link every concession involving Hormuz, sanctions or the U.S. blockade to a measurable Iranian step on the nuclear file.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The U.S. military has been enforcing a naval blockade in the Strait of Hormuz, even during the ceasefire. (U.S. Central Command)
"The best approach to ensure a solid deal is to make the nuclear issues just as important as the Strait of Hormuz, removing the blockade and other top Iranian priorities," she said.

Efrat (Effie) Lachter is a reporter for Fox News Digital with more than 15 years of experience covering conflict, global affairs, human rights and political accountability. She has directed and produced more than 200 documentary segments across more than 40 countries, documenting conflicts, humanitarian crises, corruption, human trafficking, gender-based violence and the human stories behind major world events.

Lachter’s reporting has taken her into conflict zones and crisis areas across the Middle East, Europe, Asia and Africa. Her work has included uncovering human trafficking networks, revealing an ISIS underground torture prison in Syria, documenting the war in Ukraine and interviewing senior political figures and world leaders. She was also among the Western journalists who entered Russia after the war began to bring testimonies from Putin’s opposition. Lachter is the recipient of the 2022 Peres Center for Peace Award and was a 2023–2024 Knight-Wallace Journalism Fellow at the University of Michigan. She also won two Rockower Awards for Excellence in Reporting. She holds a bachelor's degree in communication and a master's degree in political science.

title: Israeli President Herzog calls antisemitism a 'contamination of societies' as hate crimes surge
summary: NYPD data shows anti-Jewish incidents account for 56.9% of all hate crimes in 2026 as Israeli President Isaac Herzog warns antisemitism is a global contamination.
story: Israeli President Isaac Herzog says antisemitism is an "age-old plague" that harms entire societies, pointing to Holocaust denial and social media distortions as growing challenges. (Video: Yoav Dudkevitch for Fox News Digitial.)
Israeli President Isaac Herzog issued a stern warning about the global spread of antisemitism in an exclusive interview with Fox News Digital at his Jerusalem residence.
"Antisemitism is an age-old plague which should be dealt with by everybody, by all societies. It's not an Israeli issue or only a Jewish issue," he said.

"It's a contamination of societies that starts with the Jews — never ends with them. It's the most dangerous phenomena that has to be dealt with aggressively, with no mercy, with full adjudication, and most importantly, with education," he added.
EXCLUSIVE: ISRAELI PRESIDENT HERZOG BLASTS MAMDANI, PRAISES TRUMP, SOUNDS ALARM ON IRAN
Growing antisemitism and other issues led President Isaac Herzog to launch Voice of the People in April 2023. (Yoav Dudkevitch/TPS-IL for Fox News Digital)

Herzog's warning comes as newly released New York City Police Department (NYPD) data show anti-Jewish incidents accounted for 56.9% of all confirmed hate crimes since the start of 2026, even though Jewish New Yorkers make up only about 10% of the city's population.
Herzog pointed to New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani, whom he accused of spreading hate and compromising the lives of New Yorkers.

"Mamdani does not respect my nation's right for self-determination — the Jewish people's inherent right to have a nation of their own. And he's basically spreading blasphemy, hate, antisemitic rhetoric. He should understand that he's risking his own citizens, he’s risking their safety, well-being and life," Herzog told Fox News Digital.
In a video posted on social media on July 21, Mamdani called Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu "a war criminal" and "the architect of a horrific genocide against the Palestinian people."
Days later, Raul Morales, 51, allegedly yelled "Allahu Akbar" while stabbing two men on Manhattan's Upper West Side, including one who was visibly identifiable as Jewish.
SUSPECT ARRESTED AFTER ALLEGEDLY YELLING ‘ALLAHU AKBAR,' STABBING 2 MEN IN NYC ATTACK
Members of the Jewish community view the scene of an antisemitic arson attack in the Golders Green neighborhood of north London, on March 24, 2026. (Henry Nicholls/AFP via Getty Images)

"We've seen the stabbing just a few days ago... just because somebody was dressed as an Orthodox Jew. This cannot be accepted in New York, which is a city that is dear to our heart, dear to Israelis, and dear to me personally," Herzog said.

More broadly, a report released last month by the J7 Large Communities' Task Force Against Antisemitism found that 20 people were killed in antisemitic attacks across seven countries outside Israel in 2025, marking the deadliest year for such violence in the Jewish diaspora since 1994.
The J7 comprises Jewish communities in the United States, Australia, Canada, Argentina, the United Kingdom, Germany and France.
People walk through Times Square during an anti-Israel rally on Oct. 4, 2025, in New York City. (Stephanie Keith/Getty Images)

According to the report, more than 23,000 antisemitic incidents were recorded across the J7 countries last year, representing a 97% increase in violent attacks and a 136% rise in overall incidents compared with 2022.

"Of course, Israel is doing its best, but it has to be an effort with governments all over the world, law enforcement agencies, educational systems and Jewish communities, which we care about a lot," Herzog said, in reference to confronting Jew-hatred.

Referencing a recent article by professor Niall Ferguson titled "The Death of History," he said, "How much TikTok or the social networks distort the facts of history? They negate the worst and greatest horror of humankind, the Holocaust. And that's why we have to stand up together and combat it," he told Fox News Digital.
Herzog stressed that misinformation spread through distorted and superficial channels makes it easy to smear Israel on social media, but that such narratives do not reflect reality.
GERMAN OFFICIALS WARN ISLAMIST, FAR-LEFT RHETORIC DRIVING SPIKE IN ANTISEMITIC ATTACKS
Aerial view of Israel's Mediterranean coastal city Tel Aviv. (Menahem Kahana/AFP via Getty Images)
SIGN UP FOR ANTISEMITISM EXPOSED NEWSLETTER

"[Israel] is the place where the Startup Nation flourishes. This is the place where great ideas are given to the world and contribute enormously to the world in so many great fields, from health to energy, to science, to agriculture, to food security, to what not. There's a reason why Americans who visit our country, young Americans, fall in love with this country," he said.

Growing antisemitism, coupled with polarization within and between Jewish communities and a weakening sense of Jewish identity in some places, led Herzog to launch Voice of the People in April 2023. The initiative brings together a council of 150 emerging leaders — one-third from Israel, one-third from the United States and the remainder from around the world.
Leaders are selected through an algorithm from thousands of candidates and serve rotating terms of roughly two years, developing ideas to address challenges facing the Jewish world.

The initiative held an in-person kickoff summit in March 2025 in Haifa, featuring Herzog and bringing together all council members, reflecting his belief in building the next generation of Jewish leadership, which he described as one of his main tasks.

title: Capybaras crash Brazilian lawmakers' voting session and steal the show
summary: Capybaras wandered through the front door of the Mato Grosso state legislature in Brazil, surprising lawmakers preparing for a vote last week.
story: A group of capybaras has been crashing into a Brazilian state legislature's voting sessions. (UGC via AP)
Brazilian lawmakers preparing to conduct official business found themselves sharing the halls of a state legislature with several uninvited — but unusually relaxed — guests.
A group of capybaras entered the Mato Grosso Legislative Assembly in Cuiabá on July 30, briefly drawing attention away from an upcoming vote as they explored the government building.
Video recorded by legislative staffer Nayara Bueno showed the animals moving calmly through the entrance while workers sought to steer them outside.
BLACK BEAR CAUGHT ON VIDEO WANDERING INTO CALIFORNIA WATER DISTRICT OFFICE AFTER PUSHING OPEN FRONT DOOR
A group of capybaras has increasingly been crashing into a Brazilian state legislature's voting sessions. (UGC via AP)
"They show up here quite often, so we’ve gotten used to seeing them," Bueno told The Associated Press.
The rodents' guest appearance did not cause any damage to the Mato Grosso state legislature, according to officials.
The animals appeared calm as they wandered through the front door of the local legislative building in Cuiaba. (UGC via AP)
The legislature borders a park that is home to wildlife, giving the animals easy access to the surrounding government complex.

Native to South America, capybaras are semiaquatic mammals commonly found around wetlands and other bodies of water. They are highly social, generally travel in groups and can reach weights of about 175 pounds.

The legislative building is located near a park filled with wildlife, where the capybaras had wandered away from. (UGC via AP)

The world's largest living rodents have also become internet favorites, with social media users frequently highlighting their laid-back behavior around other animals and people.
